Plant Structure Outline
explanation: This slide provides an outline of the topics covered in the Plant Structure and Organization unit. The unit is divided into the following main subtopics: Organs of Flowering Plants, Tissues of Flowering Plants, Organization and Diversity of Roots, Organization and Diversity of Stems, and Organization and Diversity of Leaves.

questions.q: Which of the following topics is listed as part of the Plant Structure Outline?
opts: Organization and Diversity of Roots, Stems, and Leaves
questions.exp: The Plant Structure Outline lists 'Organs of Flowering Plants', 'Tissues of Flowering Plants', and the 'Organization and Diversity' of roots, stems, and leaves.

original_text: Organs of Flowering Plants¨We will be using the flowering plant as our model for understanding plant structure and organization. ¨Most flowering plants have a root system (made of the roots) and a shoot system (made of stem and leaves)¨Most typical plants feature 3 vegetative organs, concerned with growth and nutrition¤Roots, stems, leaves¤Flowers, seeds and fruits are involved with reproduction, not growth and nutrition.
explanation: Flowering plants serve as the standard model for studying plant structure and organization. The body of a flowering plant is divided into two primary systems: the root system (comprising the roots) and the shoot system (comprising the stem and leaves). The plant possesses three vegetative organs that are responsible for growth and nutrition: the roots, stems, and leaves. Other plant organs, specifically flowers, seeds, and fruits, are specialized structures involved in reproduction rather than vegetative growth or nutrition.

questions.q: Which of the following is considered a vegetative organ of a plant concerned with growth and nutrition?
questions.exp: The three vegetative organs concerned with plant growth and nutrition are the roots, stems, and leaves. Flowers, fruits, and seeds are involved in reproduction.

questions.q: What are the two primary systems that make up the structure of a flowering plant?
opts: The primary system and the secondary system
The vascular system and the ground system
The root system and the shoot system
The vegetative system and the reproductive system
questions.exp: Most flowering plants are structurally organized into a root system (roots) and a shoot system (stems and leaves).

original_text: Organs of Flowering Plants¨Roots¤Generally the root system is at least equivalent in size and extent to the shoot systemnAnchors plant in soilnAbsorbs water and minerals from the soilnProduces hormones¤Root hairs:nProjections from epidermal root-hair cellsnGreatly increase absorptive capacity of root¨Stems¤Shoot system of a plant is composed of the stem, branches, and leavesnStem is the main axis of a plant that elongates and produces leavesnNodesoccur where leaves are attached to the stemnInternodeis region between nodesnAxillarybuds can produce new branches of the stem (or flowers)nStem also has vascular tissue that transports water and minerals
explanation: This slide details the structure and function of roots and stems in flowering plants. The root system, which is usually equal to or larger than the shoot system in size, anchors the plant in the soil, absorbs water and minerals, and produces hormones. Root hairs, which are projections of root epidermal cells, significantly enhance the root's ability to absorb water and minerals. The shoot system includes the stem, branches, and leaves. The stem serves as the main elongating axis that produces leaves. Leaves attach to the stem at nodes, and the space between these nodes is called the internode. Axillary buds, located at the nodes, can grow into new branches or flowers. The stem contains vascular tissue to transport water, minerals, and other substances.

questions.q: What structures project from the epidermal cells of roots to increase their absorptive surface area?
questions.exp: Root hairs are cellular projections from epidermal root-hair cells that greatly increase the root's absorptive capacity.

questions.q: What is the name of the stem region located between the points where leaves are attached?
questions.exp: Nodes are the points where leaves attach to the stem, and the internode is the region between those nodes.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a main function of roots as described in the text?
opts: Elongating the main axis to produce leaves
questions.exp: Elongating the main axis to produce leaves is a function of the stem, not the roots. The roots function to anchor the plant, absorb water/minerals, and produce hormones.

Organs of Flowering Plants¨Leaves¤Major part of the plant that carries on photosynthesisnFoliage leaves are usually broad and thinnBlade-Wide portion of foliage leafnPetiole-Stalk attaching blade to stemnLeaf Axil -Upper acute angle between petiole and stem where the axillary bud is foundnTendrils-Leaves that attach to objectsnBulbs-Leaves that store food
¨Plants either categorized as monocots or eudicots (as described in Unit 6.5)
explanation: Leaves are the principal photosynthetic organs of plants. Typically broad and thin to optimize light capture, foliage leaves have two main parts: the wide blade and the petiole (the stalk that joins the blade to the stem). The upper acute angle between the petiole and stem is the leaf axil, where the axillary bud resides. Leaves can be modified for specialized tasks, such as tendrils (leaves that wrap around objects for support) and bulbs (leaves adapted for food storage). Additionally, flowering plants are broadly classified into monocots or eudicots.

questions.q: What is the name of the stalk that connects the leaf blade to the stem?
questions.exp: The petiole is the stalk that attaches the leaf blade to the stem. The blade is the wide portion of the leaf.

questions.q: Which leaf modification is correctly paired with its function?
questions.exp: Tendrils are leaves modified to attach to objects, whereas bulbs are leaves modified to store food.

original_text: Tissues of Flowering Plants¨Meristematic tissue enables flowering plants to grow throughout their lifetime¨Apical meristems at the tips of stems and roots increase the length of these tissues¨Apical meristem produces three types of meristem, which produce three specialized tissues¤Epidermal tissue¤Ground tissue¤Vascular tissue
explanation: Flowering plants display indeterminate growth throughout their lifetimes, a capability made possible by meristematic tissue. Apical meristems, found at the tips of roots and stems, are responsible for primary growth, which increases the length of these organs. The apical meristem gives rise to three transitional meristems, which subsequently differentiate into three specialized mature tissue systems: epidermal tissue (outer protective layer), ground tissue (fills the interior of the plant and performs multiple metabolic functions), and vascular tissue (transports fluids and nutrients).

questions.q: What specific tissue type allows flowering plants to grow throughout their entire lifetime?
questions.exp: Meristematic tissue consists of actively dividing cells that permit continuous, lifelong growth in flowering plants.

questions.q: Where are apical meristems located, and what is their primary function?
opts: At the nodes of stems; to produce new branches
Under the bark of woody plants; to increase plant width
At the tips of stems and roots; to increase the length of these structures
Within the vascular bundles; to facilitate transport of water and food
questions.exp: Apical meristems are situated at the tips of stems and roots, where they divide to extend the length of the plant (primary growth).

original_text: Tissues of Flowering Plants¨Epidermal Tissue¤Forms the outer protective covering of a plant¤Epidermiscontains closely packed epidermal cellsnEpidermal cells exposed to air are covered with waxy cuticlenRoot epidermal cells have root hairsnEpidermal cells of stems, leaves, and reproductive organs have trichomesnLower leaf surface contains stomata¤In older woody plants, the epidermis of the stem is replaced by peridermnMajor component is corknNew cork is made by cork cambium
explanation: Epidermal tissue forms the outermost protective envelope of the plant. In herbaceous parts, the epidermis consists of tightly packed cells. Those cells exposed to air are coated with a waxy cuticle to minimize desiccation. Specialized epidermal structures include root hairs for absorption in roots, trichomes (protective hair-like structures) on stems, leaves, and reproductive organs, and stomata (pores for gas exchange) on the lower surface of leaves. In older, woody stems, the epidermis is replaced by periderm, which is primarily composed of cork cells generated by the cork cambium.

questions.q: What substance covers the epidermal cells that are exposed to air to prevent water loss?
questions.exp: Epidermal cells exposed to air are covered with a waxy cuticle, which acts as a barrier to prevent excessive water loss.

questions.q: In older woody plants, the epidermis of the stem is replaced by which of the following protective layers?
questions.exp: In older woody plants, the epidermis is replaced by the periderm, which is composed of cork produced by the cork cambium.

questions.q: Which structures are hair-like projections found on the epidermal cells of stems, leaves, and reproductive organs?
questions.exp: Trichomes are the hair-like projections found on stems, leaves, and reproductive organs. Root hairs are located on root epidermal cells.

original_text: Tissues of Flowering Plants¨Ground tissue forms bulk of a flowering plant¤Parenchyma cells:nLeast specialized and are found in all organs of plantnCan divide and give rise to more specialized cells¤Collenchyma cells:nHave thicker primary wallsnForm bundles underneath epidermisnProvide flexible support for immature regions of the plant¤Sclerenchyma cells:nHave thick secondary walls impregnated with ligninnMost are nonlivingnPrimary function is to support mature regions of the plantnTwo types of sclerenchyma cellsnFibersnSclereids
explanation: Ground tissue forms the majority of the internal volume of a flowering plant and consists of three distinct cell types: parenchyma, collenchyma, and sclerenchyma. Parenchyma cells are the least specialized cells, are present in all plant organs, and retain the capability to divide and give rise to more specialized cells. Collenchyma cells have unevenly thickened primary cell walls and form bundles directly beneath the epidermis, providing flexible structural support to growing, immature regions of the plant. Sclerenchyma cells possess thick secondary cell walls reinforced with lignin. Most sclerenchyma cells are dead (nonliving) at functional maturity, and their primary role is to provide rigid support to mature, non-growing parts of the plant. Sclerenchyma cells are subcategorized into fibers (long, slender bundles) and sclereids (short, irregular cells).

questions.q: Which type of ground tissue cells are least specialized, present in all organs, and retain the ability to divide?
questions.exp: Parenchyma cells are the least specialized ground tissue cells, are found throughout the plant, and can divide to regenerate tissues.

questions.q: What is the primary function and characteristic of sclerenchyma cells?
opts: Provide flexible support for immature regions with thin primary walls
Divide continuously to produce secondary xylem and phloem
Provide rigid support to mature regions with thick, lignified secondary walls, and are mostly dead at maturity
Form the waxy cuticle on the outer epidermis to prevent water loss
questions.exp: Sclerenchyma cells have thick secondary walls impregnated with lignin, are mostly nonliving at maturity, and function to support mature regions of the plant.

original_text: Tissues of Flowering Plants¨Vascular Tissue¤Xylemtransports water and minerals from the roots to the leavesnTracheidsnLong, with tapered endsnWater moves across pits in end walls and side wallsnVascular rays between rows of tracheidsconduct water across the width of the plantnVessel ElementsnLarger, with perforated plates in their end wallsnForm a continuous vessel for water and mineral transport
explanation: Vascular tissue in plants is specialized for transport. Xylem is the vascular tissue responsible for conducting water and dissolved minerals from the root system upward to the leaves. It contains two main types of water-conducting cells: tracheids and vessel elements. Tracheids are elongated cells with tapered, overlapping ends. Water moves from cell to cell through pits in their end and side walls. Running between rows of tracheids are vascular rays, which function to conduct water laterally across the width of the stem or root. Vessel elements are wider cells that feature perforated plates in their end walls, aligning end-to-end to form continuous, tube-like vessel systems for efficient longitudinal water transport.

questions.q: Which conducting cells in xylem have perforated plates in their end walls and align end-to-end to form a continuous transport tube?
questions.exp: Vessel elements are larger cells with perforated plates in their end walls that form continuous tubes for water transport. Tracheids are tapered and transport water through pits.

questions.q: What is the role of vascular rays within the xylem tissue?
opts: To carry sucrose from leaves to roots
To conduct water horizontally across the width of the plant
To produce new epidermal cover in woody stems
To divide and form new tracheids
questions.exp: Vascular rays conduct water laterally (across the width of the plant) between rows of tracheids.

original_text: Tissues of Flowering Plants¨Vascular Tissue¤Phloemtransports sucrose and other organic compounds from the leaves to the rootsnSieve-tubemembersfunction as conducting cellsnContain cytoplasm, but lack nucleinSieve plate –cluster of pores in wallnEach sieve-tube member has a companion cellnPlasmodesmata connect the twonCompanion cell contains a nucleus
explanation: Phloem is the vascular tissue that transports sucrose and other organic nutrients from the leaves (sites of photosynthesis) downward to the roots and other non-photosynthetic organs. The primary conducting cells are sieve-tube members, which are living cells containing cytoplasm but lacking nuclei and most organelles at maturity to facilitate unimpeded flow. The end walls of these cells contain clusters of pores called sieve plates. Every sieve-tube member is closely associated with a adjacent companion cell, which contains a nucleus and coordinates metabolic activities for the sieve-tube member. The cytoplasm of the sieve-tube member and its companion cell are connected by intercellular junctions called plasmodesmata.

questions.q: Which of the following statements accurately describes sieve-tube members?
opts: They are dead cells that lack cytoplasm and nuclei.
They are living cells that contain cytoplasm but lack nuclei.
They are living cells that contain both nuclei and companion cells inside their cytoplasm.
They are tracheary elements with lignified secondary walls.
questions.exp: Sieve-tube members function as conducting cells that contain cytoplasm but lack nuclei at maturity. They are associated with companion cells which do have nuclei.

questions.q: What structures connect sieve-tube members to their companion cells?
questions.exp: Plasmodesmata are cytoplasmic channels that connect sieve-tube members to their companion cells, allowing exchange of materials and metabolic regulation.

original_text: Organization and Diversity of Roots¨Root cap contains root apical meristem¨Zone of cell division contains primary meristems¨Zone of elongation contains cells that are lengthening and becoming specialized¨Zone of maturation contains fully differentiated cells¨Tissues of a Eudicot Root:¤Epidermis-outer layer of root¤Cortex–composed of parenchyma cells allowing water and minerals movement¤Endodermis–forms a boundary between cortex and inner vascular cylindernCasparianstrip¤Vascular Tissue -contains xylem and phloemnPericycle–mitotically active and can begin development of branch or lateral roots
explanation: At the tip of a root, the root cap covers and protects the root apical meristem. Roots grow through three sequential zones: the zone of cell division (housing the actively dividing primary meristems), the zone of elongation (where cells lengthen and begin to specialize), and the zone of maturation (where cells fully differentiate and root hairs are formed). The primary tissues of a eudicot root include: the epidermis (outer protective layer), the cortex (composed of parenchyma cells that allow passage of water and minerals), the endodermis (a boundary layer between the cortex and the vascular cylinder featuring a waxy Casparian strip that regulates water entry), and the inner vascular cylinder. Inside the vascular cylinder is the vascular tissue (xylem and phloem) and the pericycle, a mitotically active layer of cells capable of initiating the growth of lateral or branch roots.

questions.q: Which tissue layer in eudicot roots contains the Casparian strip and regulates the movement of water and minerals into the vascular cylinder?
questions.exp: The endodermis forms the boundary between the cortex and vascular cylinder and contains the Casparian strip, which controls the entrance of substances into the vascular cylinder.

questions.q: What is the function of the pericycle in eudicot roots?
opts: It secretes the waxy Casparian strip.
It absorbs water and minerals using root hairs.
It is mitotically active and initiates lateral root development.
It transports sucrose from the shoot to the root cap.
questions.exp: The pericycle is a mitotically active layer of cells located just inside the endodermis that can divide to form branch (lateral) roots.

original_text: Organization and Diversity of Roots
explanation: This page introduces the subtopic of root organization and diversity. It serves as a divider or section title within the notes.

questions.q: Which organ system's organization and diversity is introduced on this slide?
questions.exp: The slide serves as a transition to discuss the organization and diversity of the root system.

original_text: Organization and Diversity of Roots¨Monocot roots:¤Ground tissue of root’s pithis surrounded by vascular ring¤Have the same growth zones as eudicot roots, but do not undergo secondary growth¤Have pericycle, endodermis, cortex, and epidermis
explanation: Monocot roots possess the same protective and structural tissues as eudicot roots, including the epidermis, cortex, endodermis, and pericycle, and they exhibit the same three developmental zones (cell division, elongation, and maturation). However, they differ in two main ways: monocot roots do not undergo secondary (thickening) growth, and their vascular tissues (xylem and phloem) are arranged in a ring that surrounds a central core of ground tissue called the pith.

questions.q: Which of the following is true about monocot roots?
opts: They undergo extensive secondary growth via the vascular cambium.
They lack an endodermis and pericycle.
They have a central core of ground tissue (pith) surrounded by a vascular ring.
They lack a zone of maturation and do not produce root hairs.
questions.exp: Monocot roots have a central pith composed of ground tissue, which is surrounded by a ring of vascular tissue. They do not undergo secondary growth.

original_text: Organization and Diversity of Roots¨Primary root (taproot) -Fleshy, long single root, that grows straight down¤Stores food¨Fibrous root system -Slender roots and lateral branches¤Anchors plant to soil¨Adventitious roots -Roots develop from organs of the shoot system instead of the root system¤Prop roots¨Haustoria-Found in parasitic plants¤Rootlike projections that grow into host plant¤Make contact with vascular tissue of the host plant and extract water and nutrients¨Mycorrhizae¤Mutualistic associations between roots and fungi¤Assist in water and mineral extraction¨Root nodules -Contain nitrogen-fixing bacteria
explanation: Plants possess different types of root systems and specialized root modifications adapted to various functions. A taproot (primary root) is a long, fleshy single root that grows straight downward and specializes in food storage. A fibrous root system consists of many slender roots and lateral branches that spread out to anchor the plant. Adventitious roots develop from shoot organs (like stems or leaves) instead of the primary root system; prop roots are a key example. Parasitic plants have specialized roots called haustoria that grow into the host plant to make contact with its vascular tissue and extract water and nutrients. Many plants establish mutualisms, such as mycorrhizae (associations between roots and fungi that improve water and mineral absorption) and root nodules (structures containing symbiotic nitrogen-fixing bacteria that supply nitrogen to the plant).

questions.q: What are haustoria?
opts: Symbiotic associations between roots and fungi that absorb minerals
Root-like projections of parasitic plants that tap into the host plant's vascular tissue
Underground horizontal stems used for food storage
Hormone-secreting cells located within the root cap
questions.exp: Haustoria are specialized roots of parasitic plants that penetrate the host plant to extract water and nutrients from its vascular system.

questions.q: Roots that develop from shoot structures (like stems or leaves) rather than from the root system are called:
questions.exp: Adventitious roots are roots that develop from shoot organs (such as stems or leaves) instead of the root system. Prop roots are an example.

questions.q: What is the function of root nodules?
opts: They store starch and sugars for winter survival.
They secrete waxy cutin to protect against water loss.
They house nitrogen-fixing bacteria that assist the plant.
They anchor the plant in loose, sandy soils.
questions.exp: Root nodules contain symbiotic, nitrogen-fixing bacteria that convert atmospheric nitrogen into a form the plant can utilize.

original_text: Organization and Diversity of Stems¨Shoot apical meristem¤Produces new cells that elongate and increase stem length¤Protected by terminal budnEnveloped by leaf primordianSpecialized primary meristemsnProtoderm –gives rise to the epidermisnGround Meristem –gives rise to pith and cortexnProcambium –produces primary xylem and phloem
explanation: The shoot apical meristem is the growth region located at the tip of the stem. It produces new cells that elongate to increase stem height. This meristem is protected within the terminal bud and is enveloped by leaf primordia (embryonic leaves). The shoot apical meristem differentiates into three specialized primary meristems: 1) Protoderm, which develops into the outer epidermis. 2) Ground Meristem, which gives rise to the pith and cortex. 3) Procambium, which produces the primary vascular tissues: xylem and phloem.

questions.q: Which primary meristem differentiates into the pith and the cortex?
questions.exp: The ground meristem gives rise to the pith and cortex, whereas the protoderm forms the epidermis, and the procambium forms vascular tissue.

questions.q: What structures envelop and protect the delicate shoot apical meristem?
questions.exp: Leaf primordia are embryonic leaves that envelope and protect the shoot apical meristem inside the terminal bud.

original_text: Organization and Diversity of Stems¨Herbaceous Stems¤Mature non-woody stems exhibit only primary growthnOutermost tissue covered with waxy cuticlenStems have distinctive vascular bundlesnHerbaceous eudicots -Vascular bundles arranged in distinct ringnMonocots -Vascular bundles scattered throughout stem
explanation: Herbaceous stems are mature, non-woody stems that undergo only primary growth (growth in length). The outer surface is covered with a waxy cuticle that limits water loss. The vascular tissues in herbaceous stems are grouped into vascular bundles. The spatial arrangement of these bundles differs between monocots and eudicots: in herbaceous eudicot stems, the vascular bundles are organized in a distinct ring; in monocots, the vascular bundles are scattered randomly throughout the ground tissue of the stem.

questions.q: How do vascular bundles differ in arrangement between monocot stems and herbaceous eudicot stems?
opts: Monocots have vascular bundles arranged in a distinct ring, while eudicots have them scattered.
Monocots have vascular bundles scattered throughout the stem, while herbaceous eudicots have them arranged in a distinct ring.
Monocots lack vascular bundles entirely, while eudicots have them in a central core.
Both have scattered bundles, but monocots lack a protective cuticle.
questions.exp: In monocot stems, vascular bundles are scattered throughout the stem. In herbaceous eudicots, vascular bundles are arranged in a distinct ring.

questions.q: What type of growth is exhibited by mature herbaceous stems?
questions.exp: Herbaceous stems are non-woody and exhibit only primary growth (lengthwise growth).

original_text: Organization of Diversity of Stems¨Woody Stems¤Woody plants have both primary and secondary tissuesnPrimary tissues formed each year from primary meristemsnSecondary tissues develop during first and subsequent years from lateral meristems¤Woody stems have both primary and secondary growthnPrimary growth increases the length of the plantnSecondary growth increases the girth¤Woody stems have no vascular tissue, and instead have three distinct regionsnBarknWoodnPith
explanation: Woody stems undergo both primary growth (which increases plant length) and secondary growth (which increases girth/thickness). They possess both primary tissues (formed annually from apical and primary meristems) and secondary tissues (developed starting in their first year and in subsequent years from lateral meristems: vascular cambium and cork cambium). In mature woody stems, individual vascular bundles are no longer present. Instead, the stem is organized into three distinct concentric regions: bark (outer layers), wood (secondary xylem), and a central pith.

questions.q: In a woody stem, which type of growth is responsible for increasing the girth (thickness)?
questions.exp: Secondary growth increases the girth (width/thickness) of the stem, whereas primary growth increases length.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the three distinct anatomical regions of a mature woody stem?
questions.exp: Woody stems do not contain discrete vascular bundles; instead, the tissues are organized into bark, wood, and pith.

original_text: Organization and Diversity of Stems¨Bark¤Bark of a tree contains cork, cork cambium, and phloem¤Bark can be removed, but it is harmful to the plant due to lack of organic nutrient transport¤Cork cells are impregnated with suberinnGas exchange is impeded except at lenticels¨Wood¤Wood is secondary xylem that builds up year after yearnVascular cambium is dormant during winternAnnual ring is made up of spring wood and summer wood¤In older trees, inner annual rings, called heartwood, no longer function in water transport
explanation: This slide details the structure of bark and wood in woody stems. Bark is the outermost protective region containing cork, cork cambium, and phloem. Removing bark (girdling) is highly damaging or fatal because it removes the phloem, interrupting the transport of organic nutrients. Cork cells are impregnated with a waxy, waterproof material called suberin, which blocks gas exchange except at specialized pores called lenticels. Wood consists of layers of secondary xylem that accumulate annually. The vascular cambium (the lateral meristem that produces secondary xylem) is dormant in winter. An annual ring consists of spring wood (rapidly grown, wider xylem cells) and summer wood (slower grown, thick-walled, narrower xylem cells). In older trees, the oldest inner rings of xylem clog and stop transporting water; this non-functional wood is known as heartwood.

questions.q: Why is removing the bark of a tree extremely harmful to the plant?
opts: It removes the wood, stopping water transport.
It removes the phloem, stopping organic nutrient transport.
It exposes the heartwood to fungal infection.
It destroys the apical meristem at the stem tip.
questions.exp: Bark contains the phloem. Removing bark destroys the phloem layer, preventing the transport of sucrose and other organic nutrients to the roots.

questions.q: What is the function of lenticels in bark?
opts: To allow gas exchange through the suberin-impregnated cork layer
To absorb water from the air
questions.exp: Cork cells are impregnated with suberin, which is impermeable to gases. Lenticels are specialized pores that allow gas exchange through this barrier.

questions.q: What is heartwood?
opts: The soft ground tissue at the center of a woody stem (pith)
The active, outermost ring of secondary xylem
The non-functional, older inner annual rings of secondary xylem
The layers of bark that are shed each year
questions.exp: Heartwood consists of the older, inner annual rings of secondary xylem that no longer function in water transport.

original_text: Organization and Diversity of Stems¨Above ground vertical stems¨Stolons¤Above ground horizontal stems¤Produce new plants when nodes touch the ground¨Rhizomes¤Underground horizontal stems¤Contribute to asexual reproduction¤Variations:nTubers -Enlarged portions functioning in food storagenCorms -Underground stems that produce new plants during the next season
explanation: Stems are modified for asexual reproduction and nutrient storage. 1) Stolons (or runners) are horizontal stems that grow above the ground and produce new clone plants at their nodes when they make contact with the soil. 2) Rhizomes are horizontal stems that grow underground, contributing to asexual reproduction. 3) Tubers are swollen, enlarged sections of underground stems (either rhizomes or stolons) specialized for food storage (e.g., potatoes). 4) Corms are bulb-like, thickened underground stems that store nutrients to produce new shoots during the following growing season.

questions.q: Which stem modification is defined as an above-ground horizontal stem that forms new plants where its nodes touch the ground?
questions.exp: Stolons are above-ground horizontal stems that produce new clone plants when their nodes contact the soil. Rhizomes are underground horizontal stems.

questions.q: What is a tuber (such as a white potato)?
opts: A swollen root specialized for water absorption
An enlarged portion of an underground stem specialized for food storage
A vertical, above-ground stem used for climbing
A leaf modification that wraps around objects
questions.exp: Tubers are enlarged portions of underground stems (rhizomes or stolons) that store food.

original_text: Organization and Diversity of Leaves¨Leaves contain:¤Upper and lower epidermisnWaxy cuticlenTrichomesnLower epidermis has stomata for gas exchange¤MesophyllnEudicot leaves havenPalisade mesophyll containing elongated cellsnSpongy mesophyll containing irregular cells bounded by air spacesnContains many chloroplasts
explanation: The anatomy of a leaf is specialized for photosynthesis and gas exchange. The leaf is bounded by an upper and lower epidermis. These epidermal layers are covered with a waxy cuticle to prevent water loss and may feature trichomes. The lower epidermis features stomata, microscopic pores that regulate gas exchange. The internal tissue of the leaf is the mesophyll, which contains numerous chloroplasts. In eudicot leaves, the mesophyll is differentiated into two layers: 1) Palisade mesophyll: located below the upper epidermis, consisting of tightly packed, column-like elongated cells optimized for light absorption. 2) Spongy mesophyll: located above the lower epidermis, consisting of loosely packed, irregularly shaped cells surrounded by extensive air spaces that facilitate the diffusion of gases.

questions.q: In a eudicot leaf, which layer contains tightly packed, elongated cells beneath the upper epidermis?
questions.exp: The palisade mesophyll contains tightly packed, elongated cells beneath the upper epidermis, specialized for absorbing light. Spongy mesophyll contains irregular cells with air spaces.

questions.q: Where are stomata typically located, and what is their primary function in leaves?
opts: In the upper epidermis; to secrete the waxy cuticle
In the lower epidermis; to allow gas exchange
In the spongy mesophyll; to store starch
In the vascular bundle; to transport water
questions.exp: Stomata are pores located primarily on the lower epidermis of leaves to facilitate gas exchange while minimizing water loss.

original_text: Organization and Diversity of Leaves¨Leaf Diversity¤Blade of a leaf can be simple or compound¤Leaves are adapted to environmental conditionsnShade leavesnSpinesnClimbing leaves
explanation: Leaf morphology is highly diverse and adapted to different environmental conditions. The blade of a leaf can be simple (a single, undivided leaf blade) or compound (divided into multiple distinct leaflets). Leaves also undergo modifications to suit specific habitats: 1) Shade leaves: broader and thinner leaves that maximize light capture in low-light environments. 2) Spines: reduced, sharp leaves that protect the plant from herbivores and minimize water loss (e.g., in cacti). 3) Climbing leaves: modified to wrap around structures to support the plant's vertical growth (acting like tendrils).

questions.q: A leaf whose blade is divided into multiple separate leaflets is called a:
questions.exp: A compound leaf has a blade that is divided into separate leaflets. A simple leaf has an undivided blade.

questions.q: Which leaf modification is adapted to protect the plant and minimize water loss in arid environments?
questions.exp: Spines are modified leaves with reduced surface area that protect the plant and reduce transpirational water loss.

Soil & Nutrition¨Water and carbon dioxide are critical components of plant nutrition ¤95% of plants dry weight C, H, or O¨Other essential nutrients must be taken up by the plants roots¤Minerals-inorganic substance usually containing 2 or more elementsnEssential nutrients have 1) an identifiable role in the plant, 2) cannot be replaced by another nutrient, and 3) a deficiency causes death. nBroken down into Macro v Micronutrients based on relative concentrations in plant tissue
¨Beneficial nutrients are required for growth, or enhance growth of a particular plant
explanation: Water and carbon dioxide are crucial for plant nutrition, as carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen (C, H, or O) make up 95% of a plant's dry weight. Other essential nutrients, such as mineral ions (inorganic substances typically consisting of two or more elements), must be absorbed from the soil by the plant's roots. A nutrient is defined as essential if it meets three criteria: 1) it has a specific, identifiable role in plant physiology, 2) it cannot be substituted by another nutrient, and 3) a deficiency in this nutrient leads to plant death. These essential nutrients are classified as macronutrients or micronutrients based on their relative concentrations in plant tissue. Additionally, some plants require or benefit from beneficial nutrients, which enhance growth but do not meet the full criteria of essentiality for all plants.

questions.q: What elements constitute approximately 95% of a plant's dry weight?
opts: Nitrogen, Phosphorus, and Potassium (N, P, K)
Carbon, Hydrogen, and Oxygen (C, H, O)
Calcium, Magnesium, and Sulfur (Ca, Mg, S)
Iron, Manganese, and Copper (Fe, Mn, Cu)
questions.exp: Water and carbon dioxide supply Carbon, Hydrogen, and Oxygen, which together make up about 95% of a plant's dry weight.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a criterion for a plant nutrient to be classified as 'essential'?
opts: It must have an identifiable role in the plant.
It cannot be replaced by another nutrient.
It must be present in concentrations greater than 10% in the soil.
A deficiency in it causes the death of the plant.
questions.exp: The three criteria are: having an identifiable role, being irreplaceable by another nutrient, and deficiency causing death. Soil concentration is not part of the criteria.

original_text: Soil & Nutrients¨Hydroponics main method of determining essential nutrients¤Grow in presence and absence of each mineral¤Most effective for Macronutrients¨These nutrients are taken in by plants at the roots, through the soil
explanation: Hydroponics is the primary experimental method used to determine whether a mineral is an essential nutrient. By growing plants in water solutions in the presence or absence of specific minerals, scientists can observe deficiency symptoms. This technique is most effective for identifying macronutrients, which are required in larger quantities. In natural settings, plants absorb these essential nutrients from the soil through their root systems.

questions.q: What is the primary method used to determine if a specific mineral is an essential nutrient for plant growth?
questions.exp: Hydroponics (growing plants in water solutions with or without specific minerals) is the main method used to test for essential nutrients, especially macronutrients.

original_text: Soil & Nutrients¨Soil¤Mixture of mineral particles, decaying organic matter, living organisms, air, and water¤All soil contains a mix of three different sized particlesnSand –Largest, most open space and drainagenSilt –Intermediate size and drainagenClay –Smallest particles, hold water with little room for air¤Humus–decaying organic matternMixes with top layer of soil, increases benefitsnPlants do well in soil containing minimum 10—20% humus¤Living OrganismsnLarge plants break soil and make room for small plantsnAnimals (toads, snakes, moles, worms, ants, etc.) mix soil as they dig and loosen layersnMicroorganisms (bacteria, fungi, protozoans) responsible for final decomposition
explanation: Soil is a heterogeneous mixture of mineral particles, decaying organic matter (humus), living organisms, air, and water. The mineral component consists of three particle sizes: sand (largest, provides optimal space and drainage), silt (intermediate size and drainage), and clay (smallest, retains water but leaves little space for air). Humus is decaying organic matter that mixes with the topsoil to increase nutrient availability and soil structure; plants grow best in soil containing a minimum of 10-20% humus. Living organisms contribute to soil health: large plants break up soil layers, digging animals (like moles, worms, ants, toads, and snakes) loosen and mix soil, and microorganisms (bacteria, fungi, and protozoans) carry out the final decomposition of organic matter.

questions.q: Which soil particle type is the smallest and retains water effectively but provides very little space for air?
questions.exp: Clay particles are the smallest, allowing them to hold water tightly, but they leave very little room for air. Sand is the largest and clay the smallest.

questions.q: What is humus, and what is the minimum percentage of it recommended in soil for optimal plant growth?
opts: A mixture of sand and silt; 50%
questions.exp: Humus is decaying organic matter. Plants thrive in soil containing a minimum of 10-20% humus.

questions.q: Which group of soil organisms is primarily responsible for the final decomposition of organic matter?
opts: Digging animals like moles and worms
questions.exp: Microorganisms, including bacteria, fungi, and protozoans, are responsible for the final decomposition of organic matter in the soil.

Water & Mineral Uptake¨Water and minerals all taken up from soil using same pathway¤Water enters root hairs when the osmotic pressure in the root is lower than found in the soil (osmosis)¤Minerals can be taken in at much higher concentration than found in soil by use of pumps to move ions 
¨Water and minerals move up xylem, from root to leaves, by upward movement of water ¨Minerals can exit xylem and enter cells requiring the nutrients along the way
explanation: Water and mineral ions enter roots via the same pathway. Water enters root hairs passively by osmosis when the osmotic pressure inside the root cells is lower than in the surrounding soil. In contrast, mineral ions can be accumulated in the root cells at concentrations much higher than those in the soil. This active accumulation is accomplished via transport pumps that move ions across membranes. Once absorbed, water and minerals enter the xylem and are transported upward from roots to leaves. Along this pathway, minerals can exit the xylem vessels and enter cells that require these nutrients.

questions.q: Under what condition does water enter root hairs from the soil via osmosis?
opts: When the osmotic pressure in the root is lower than in the soil
When the osmotic pressure in the root is higher than in the soil
When active transport pumps force water against its gradient
When the soil is completely dry
questions.exp: Water enters root hairs passively when the osmotic pressure in the root is lower than that in the soil, allowing osmosis to occur.

questions.q: How do plants transport minerals into roots at concentrations higher than those found in the soil?
opts: Through passive diffusion across the cuticle
By using specialized transport pumps to actively move ions
By converting minerals into organic gases
questions.exp: Plants use energy-dependent active transport pumps to move mineral ions into root cells, accumulating them against their concentration gradient.

original_text: Water & Mineral Uptake¨Some plants have adaptations or mutualistic relationships with other organisms to assist with water and mineral uptake¤RhizobiumbacterianCan live in root nodules on plants, and break down nitrogen. Receive carbohydrates from plant in return¤MycorrhizaenMutualistic between plant roots and fungusnAlmost ALL plants have mycorrhizaenIncrease surface area of root system for plants, and break down organic matter in soil, freeing up nutrients for plantnRoot provides sugars and amino acids for fungus¤Other methods much less commonnParasitic plants tap into other plant xylem (dodders, pinedrops)nCarnivorous plants capture and digest insects (Venus flytrap)
explanation: Plants exhibit adaptations and mutualisms to facilitate water and nutrient acquisition. Rhizobium bacteria form symbiotic associations with certain plants, residing in root nodules where they break down (fix) atmospheric nitrogen; in return, the plant provides the bacteria with carbohydrates. Mycorrhizae are mutualistic associations between plant roots and fungi, present in almost all plant species. Fungal hyphae increase the root surface area for water and mineral absorption and decompose organic matter in the soil to release nutrients; the plant root supplies the fungus with sugars and amino acids. Less common nutritional adaptations include parasitic plants (such as dodders and pinedrops) that tap into the xylem of host plants to extract nutrients, and carnivorous plants (such as the Venus flytrap) that capture and digest insects to obtain nitrogen in nutrient-poor environments.

questions.q: In the mutualism between Rhizobium bacteria and plants, what do the bacteria receive from the plant?
questions.exp: Rhizobium bacteria fix nitrogen for the plant and receive carbohydrates (sugars) in return.

questions.q: What is the primary function of mycorrhizae in plant nutrition?
opts: They capture and digest insects to supply nitrogen.
They tap into host xylem to steal water.
They increase root surface area and break down organic matter to free up nutrients.
They produce root nodules to house nitrogen-fixing bacteria.
questions.exp: Mycorrhizae (fungus-root associations) enhance water and mineral absorption by expanding root surface area and digesting soil organic matter.

questions.q: Which of the following is a parasitic plant that extracts nutrients by tapping into the xylem of a host plant?
questions.exp: Dodders and pinedrops are parasitic plants that tap into the vascular systems of host plants to acquire nutrients.

original_text: Transport Mechanisms¨Vascular tissues transport water and nutrients.¤Xylemtransports water and minerals.nTwo types of conducting cellsnTracheidsnVessel elementsnWater flows passively from an area of higher water potential to an area of lower water potential.¤Phloemtransports organic materials.nConducting cells are sieve-tube members.nThey have companion cells to provide proteins.nEnd walls are sieve plates.nPlasmodesmata extend through sieve plates.
explanation: Plant vascular tissues are specialized for the transport of fluids and nutrients. Xylem transports water and dissolved mineral ions upward from roots to shoots. It contains two types of dead conducting cells: tracheids and vessel elements. Water transport in the xylem is passive, flowing from regions of higher water potential to regions of lower water potential. Phloem transports organic compounds (such as sucrose) throughout the plant. Its conducting cells are sieve-tube members, which lack nuclei at maturity and are supported by companion cells that supply them with proteins. The end walls of sieve-tube members are called sieve plates, which feature pores through which cytoplasmic strands (plasmodesmata) connect adjacent cells.

questions.q: Water flows passively through the xylem from areas of:
opts: Lower water potential to higher water potential
Higher water potential to lower water potential
Higher solute concentration to lower solute concentration
questions.exp: Water moves passively from regions of higher water potential to regions of lower water potential.

questions.q: What structures extend through the pores in sieve plates to connect adjacent sieve-tube members?
questions.exp: Plasmodesmata are cytoplasmic strands that extend through the pores of sieve plates, connecting adjacent sieve-tube members.

original_text: Transport Mechanisms¨Pressure potential is the effect that pressure has on water potential.¤Water moves across a membrane from the area of higher pressure to the area of lower pressure.¤The higher the water pressure, the higher the water potential.¤Pressure potential that increases due to osmosis is called turgor pressure.¨Osmotic potential takes into account the presence of solutes.¤Water tends to move from the area of lower solute concentration to the area of higher solute concentration.¤The lower the concentration of solutes (osmotic potential), the higher the water potential.
explanation: Water potential, which determines the direction of water movement, is affected by pressure potential and osmotic potential. Pressure potential refers to the physical pressure on water. Water moves across membranes from areas of higher physical pressure to areas of lower physical pressure; thus, higher water pressure increases water potential. Turgor pressure is the specific pressure potential that increases inside a plant cell as water enters by osmosis, pressing the plasma membrane against the cell wall. Osmotic potential accounts for solute concentrations. Water moves from regions of lower solute concentration to regions of higher solute concentration. Consequently, a lower concentration of solutes (which corresponds to a higher osmotic potential in terms of water availability) results in a higher water potential.

questions.q: What is turgor pressure?
opts: The negative pressure potential that pulls water up the stem
The pressure potential that increases due to osmosis inside a plant cell
The pressure exerted by solutes moving out of the companion cell
The atmospheric pressure surrounding the leaves
questions.exp: Turgor pressure is the pressure potential that increases within a plant cell due to the osmotic entry of water.

questions.q: How does solute concentration affect water potential?
opts: Higher solute concentration increases water potential.
Solute concentration has no impact on water potential.
Lower solute concentration increases water potential.
Lower solute concentration decreases water potential.
questions.exp: A lower solute concentration results in a higher water potential, driving water movement toward areas of higher solute concentration.

original_text: Transport Mechanisms¨Water Transport¤Xylem vessels form an open pipeline.nThe vessel elements are separated by perforated plates.nWater moves into and out of tracheidsthrough pits.¤Water entering roots creates a positive pressure (root pressure).nIt pushes xylem sap upward.nMay be responsible for guttationnWater forced out vein endings along edges of leaves
explanation: Xylem vessels function as an open pipeline for water transport, consisting of vessel elements aligned end-to-end and separated by perforated plates. Water also moves into and out of tracheids via pits. When water enters root cells, it generates a positive hydrostatic pressure known as root pressure, which pushes xylem sap upward. Under conditions of high soil moisture and low transpiration (such as at night), root pressure can force liquid water out of specialized vein endings at the edges of leaves, a process known as guttation.

questions.q: What is guttation?
opts: The evaporation of water from the stomata during the day
The transport of sucrose from leaves to roots in phloem
The forcing of liquid water out of vein endings at leaf margins due to root pressure
The entry of water into root hairs by active transport
questions.exp: Guttation is the release of liquid water droplets from vein endings at leaf margins, caused by positive root pressure when transpiration is low.

questions.q: How does water enter and exit tracheid cells?
opts: Through perforated plates in their end walls
questions.exp: In tracheids, water moves in and out through pits in their end and side walls, unlike vessel elements which have perforated plates.

original_text: Transport Mechanisms¨Cohesion-tension model of xylem transport suggests a passive xylem transport.¤Cohesion is the tendency of water molecules to cling together.¤Adhesion is the ability of the polar water molecules to interact with molecules of vessel walls¤A continuous water column moves passively upward due to transpiration.¨Leaves¤Transpirationcauses water loss through stomata.¤Water molecules that evaporate are replaced by water molecules from leaf veins.¤Due to cohesion, transpiration exerts a pulling force (tension) drawing water through the xylem to the leaf cells.¤Waxy cuticle prevents water loss when stomata are closed.¨Stem¤Tension in xylem pulls the water column upward.¨Roots¤Water enters xylem passively by osmosis and is pulled upward due to tension in xylem.
explanation: The cohesion-tension model describes the passive transport of water through xylem. Cohesion is the attraction between polar water molecules that allows them to cling together, forming a continuous water column. Adhesion is the interaction of polar water molecules with the cellulose walls of xylem vessels, preventing the water column from slipping downward. In the leaves, transpiration (water loss by evaporation through stomata) creates tension (a pulling force) because evaporating water molecules must be replaced by water from leaf veins. Due to cohesion, this tension pulls the entire water column upward through the stem xylem. In the roots, water enters the xylem passively by osmosis and is pulled upward by this same transpirational tension. When stomata are closed, a waxy cuticle on the leaf surface prevents excessive water loss.

questions.q: What is the difference between cohesion and adhesion in xylem transport?
opts: Cohesion is water molecules clinging to each other; adhesion is water molecules interacting with vessel walls.
Cohesion is water molecules interacting with vessel walls; adhesion is water molecules clinging to each other.
Cohesion is the active pumping of water; adhesion is passive water movement.
Cohesion occurs in roots; adhesion occurs only in leaves.
questions.exp: Cohesion refers to water molecules binding to each other. Adhesion refers to water molecules binding to the cell walls of the xylem vessels.

questions.q: What generates the tension (pulling force) that drives water upward according to the cohesion-tension model?
opts: Active pumping of water by root hairs
The opening of lenticels in the bark
High solute concentration in the xylem
questions.exp: Evaporation of water (transpiration) from the leaves creates a negative pressure (tension) that pulls the water column upward.

questions.q: Which leaf structure acts to limit water loss when the stomata are closed?
questions.exp: The waxy cuticle on the leaf epidermis prevents water loss when the stomata are closed.

original_text: Transport Mechanisms¨Opening and Closing of Stomata:¤Each stoma in a leaf epidermis is bordered by guard cells.nIncreased turgor pressure in guard cells opens stoma.nActive transport of K+ into guard cells causes water to enter by osmosis and stomata to open.nH+ ions accumulate outside guard cells as K+ moves in.nOpening and closing of stomata is regulated by light.nABA (abscisic acid) can also cause stomata to close.
explanation: Stomata are bordered by pairs of guard cells that control their opening and closing. An increase in turgor pressure inside the guard cells causes them to swell and bow outward, opening the pore. This turgor pressure increase is driven by the active transport of potassium ions (K+) into the guard cells, which prompts water to follow passively by osmosis. As K+ ions enter the cells, hydrogen ions (H+) are transported out and accumulate in the surrounding tissue. Stomatal movement is regulated by environmental factors such as light. Additionally, the plant hormone abscisic acid (ABA) can trigger K+ efflux from guard cells, causing water loss, a decrease in turgor pressure, and stomatal closure to prevent water loss during stress.

questions.q: What cellular event triggers the opening of stomata?
opts: Active transport of K+ out of guard cells
Active transport of K+ into guard cells, followed by osmotic water entry
Accumulation of ABA inside guard cells
Decreased turgor pressure in guard cells
questions.exp: Active transport of potassium ions (K+) into guard cells lowers their solute potential, causing water to enter via osmosis. This increases turgor pressure and opens the stoma.

questions.q: Which plant hormone is responsible for closing stomata during water stress?
questions.exp: Abscisic acid (ABA) is the hormone that signals stomata to close to conserve water during periods of stress.

original_text: Transport Mechanisms¨Organic Nutrient Transport:¤Role of phloemnPhloem transports sugar.nPhloem sap doesn’t only move upward or downward as xylem does.nTravels from source (sugar’s origin) to sink (sugars are unloaded)nGirdling of tree below the level of leaves causes bark to swell just above the cut.nSugar accumulates in the swollen tissue.nRadioactive tracer studies confirm that phloem transports organic nutrients.nPhloem sap can be collected using aphids.
explanation: Phloem transports sucrose and other organic nutrients throughout the plant. Unlike xylem transport, which is strictly upward, phloem sap moves in multiple directions from a source (where sugar is produced or mobilized) to a sink (where sugar is unloaded and consumed or stored). Girdling (removing a strip of bark around a tree trunk) removes the phloem but leaves the xylem intact, causing the bark to swell just above the cut as sugars accumulate. Radioactive tracer studies (such as using carbon-14) have confirmed that phloem is the tissue that transports organic compounds. Researchers can collect pure phloem sap by utilizing aphids, insects that insert their mouthparts (stylets) directly into sieve-tube members.

questions.q: In phloem transport, how is the direction of sap flow determined?
opts: Unidirectionally from the roots to the leaves
Multidirectionally from a sugar source to a sugar sink
Unidirectionally from the leaves to the roots only
Randomly, depending on wind and gravity
questions.exp: Phloem transport is multidirectional, moving from sugar sources (like photosynthetic leaves) to sugar sinks (like growing roots, stems, or fruits).

questions.q: What happens when a tree trunk is girdled (a ring of bark is removed)?
opts: Water transport stops immediately, causing the leaves to wilt.
The tree grows faster because minerals accumulate in the roots.
Organic nutrients accumulate above the cut, causing the bark to swell.
questions.exp: Bark contains phloem. Girdling removes the phloem, preventing organic nutrients from moving down past the cut, which causes them to accumulate and swell the bark above it.

questions.q: How can researchers collect pure phloem sap from plants?
opts: By cutting open xylem vessel elements
By using aphids to tap into sieve-tube members
By performing hydroponic extractions on roots
questions.exp: Aphids feed by inserting their stylets directly into sieve-tube members. Researchers cut the aphid's mouthparts to collect pure phloem sap flowing under pressure.

original_text: Transport Mechanisms ¨Pressure-Flow Model of Phloem Transport¤Sieve tubes form a continuous pathway for organic nutrient transport.nSieve-tube members are aligned end to end.nStrands of plasmodesmata extend through sieve plates between sieve-tube members.¤Positive pressure drives the movement of sap in sieve tubes.nSucrose is actively transported into phloem at the leaves.nWater follows by osmosis, creating positive pressure.nThe increase in pressure causes flow that moves water and sucrose from the source to the sink (From leaves down to roots for storage)
explanation: The pressure-flow model explains the bulk flow of organic nutrients in phloem. Sieve tubes form a continuous pathway, consisting of sieve-tube members aligned end-to-end and connected by sieve plates containing pores through which strands of plasmodesmata extend. Sap movement is driven by positive hydrostatic pressure. At the source (e.g., leaves), sucrose is actively loaded into the sieve-tube members, which lowers their water potential. Water then enters the phloem from the xylem by osmosis, creating high positive pressure at the source. This high pressure forces the sap (water and sucrose) to flow toward the sink (e.g., roots), where sucrose is unloaded and water exits, maintaining the pressure gradient.

questions.q: According to the pressure-flow model, what causes the build-up of positive pressure at the source?
opts: Active pumping of water by roots
Active loading of sucrose, followed by the entry of water via osmosis
questions.exp: Sucrose is actively loaded into sieve-tube members at the source. This lowers water potential, causing water to follow by osmosis and generate high positive hydrostatic pressure.

questions.q: Where does the water that enters the phloem at the source come from?
opts: It is absorbed directly from the atmosphere.
It comes from the xylem by osmosis.
It is released by companion cells.
questions.exp: When sucrose is loaded into the phloem, water moves from the nearby xylem into the phloem by osmosis due to the concentration gradient.

original_text: Plant Hormones¨Flowering plants respond to environmental stimuli ¤Stimuli include light, gravity, carbon dioxide levels, pathogen infection, drought, and touch ¤Response to stimuli leads to the survival of the species ¨The responses can be: ¤Short term nStomata open and close in response to light levels.¤Long term nThe response to gravity causes downward growth of the root and the upward growth of the stem¨Response of plants to environmental stimuli involves signal transduction ¤The binding of a molecular “signal” that initiates and amplifies a response.
explanation: Flowering plants respond to environmental stimuli (including light, gravity, carbon dioxide levels, pathogen infection, drought, and touch) to ensure species survival. These responses can be short-term, such as guard cells opening and closing stomata in response to changing light levels, or long-term, such as gravitropism causing roots to grow downward and stems to grow upward. Environmental responses involve signal transduction, a process in which the binding of a molecular signal (hormone or environmental trigger) to a receptor initiates and amplifies a cellular response cascade.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of a long-term response of a plant to an environmental stimulus?
opts: Stomata opening and closing in response to light
Growth of the root downward and stem upward in response to gravity
Rapid trapping of an insect by a Venus flytrap
Active pumping of K+ ions into guard cells
questions.exp: Gravitropism (downward growth of roots and upward growth of stems) is a long-term growth response, while stomatal opening/closing is a short-term response.

questions.q: What is signal transduction in plant biology?
opts: The physical transport of sucrose through phloem sieve tubes
The process where a molecular signal binds to a receptor to initiate and amplify a response
The evaporation of water from leaves during transpiration
The mechanical mixing of soil by burrowing animals
questions.exp: Signal transduction involves a molecular signal binding to a receptor, which triggers and amplifies a pathway leading to a cellular response.

original_text: Plant Hormones¨Signal transduction involves the following: ¤Receptors-proteins activated by a specific signal; usually found on cell exterior¤Transduction pathway –a series of relay proteins or enzymes that amplify and transform the signal to one understood by the machinery of the cell ¤Cellular response –the result of the transduction pathway
explanation: Signal transduction in plants is the cellular process that links an environmental stimulus or chemical messenger to a physiological response. This process consists of three main components: 1) Receptors: proteins, typically located on the outer surface of the cell membrane, that are activated when they bind to a specific molecular signal. 2) Transduction pathway: a series of intracellular relay proteins or enzymes that amplify and convert the signal into a molecular message that the cell's internal machinery can interpret. 3) Cellular response: the physical, physiological, or biochemical result of the transduction pathway, such as alterations in gene expression or enzyme activity.

questions.q: Which part of the signal transduction pathway is responsible for amplifying and transforming a signal inside the cell?
questions.exp: The transduction pathway consists of a series of relay proteins or enzymes that amplify and transform the signal so the cell's machinery can act on it.

questions.q: Where are the receptor proteins in plant signal transduction typically located?
opts: On the exterior of the cell
In the center of the pith
questions.exp: Receptor proteins are typically located on the cell exterior (cell membrane) to detect incoming chemical signals.

original_text: Plant Hormones¨Hormones ¤Chemical signal to coordinate cell responses; Enable plant cells to communicate nAre usually synthesized in one part of the plant nTravel within phloem or from cell to cell in response to the appropriate stimulus¨5 main types of plant hormones¤Auxins¤Gibberellins¤Cytokinins¤Abscisic Acid¤Ethylene
explanation: Plant hormones are chemical messengers that coordinate cell responses and facilitate communication between cells. They are typically synthesized in one part of the plant and transported to other regions via the phloem or through cell-to-cell movement in response to specific stimuli. The five primary classes of plant hormones are auxins, gibberellins, cytokinins, abscisic acid (ABA), and ethylene.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the five primary classes of plant hormones?
questions.exp: The five main types of plant hormones are auxins, gibberellins, cytokinins, abscisic acid, and ethylene. Systemin is a polypeptide defense signal, not one of the five classic hormones.

questions.q: How do plant hormones typically move through the plant body?
opts: Within the phloem or from cell to cell
questions.exp: Hormones are typically synthesized in one location and travel through the phloem or pass from cell to cell to reach target tissues.

original_text: Plant Hormones¨Auxins ¤Produced in shoot apical meristem ¤Found in young leaves, flowers, and fruits ¨Effects of auxin on growth and development:¤Apically produced auxin prevents the growth of axillary buds nApical dominance –terminal growth dominant¤Promotes growth of roots and fruit ¤Prevents loss of leaves and fruit ¤Promotes positive phototropism of stems¨Auxins can cause stems to bend ¤When a stem is exposed to unidirectional light, auxin moves to the shady sides ¤Auxin binds to plasma membrane receptors; the complex leads to the activation of a proton pump ¤Activated proton pumps H+out of cell nCell wall loosens nTurgor pressure increases due to the entry of water nCell enlarges
explanation: Auxins are key plant hormones produced in the shoot apical meristem and found in young leaves, flowers, and fruits. Auxin establishes apical dominance, where auxin produced at the shoot tip inhibits the growth of axillary buds, prioritizing vertical terminal growth. Auxin also promotes root and fruit development, prevents the premature loss (abscission) of leaves and fruit, and drives positive phototropism in stems. Under unidirectional light, auxin migrates to the shaded side of the stem. It binds to membrane receptors, triggering proton pumps to actively pump hydrogen ions ($H^+$) out of the cell into the cell wall. This acidic environment loosens the cell wall structure (Acid Growth Hypothesis). Consequently, water enters the cell due to osmosis, increasing turgor pressure and causing the cells on the shady side to elongate, which bends the stem toward the light.

questions.q: What is the mechanism by which auxin causes cells to elongate during phototropism?
opts: It stimulates the active transport of water out of cells.
It activates proton pumps, pumping H+ out of the cell to loosen the cell wall so turgor pressure can enlarge it.
It deposits secondary lignin to harden the cell wall.
It triggers cell division in the cork cambium.
questions.exp: Auxin activates proton pumps to pump H+ out of the cell. This loosens the cell wall, allowing water to enter by osmosis, increasing turgor pressure and expanding the cell.

questions.q: What term describes the phenomenon where auxin produced at the stem tip prevents the growth of axillary buds?
questions.exp: Apical dominance is the suppression of lateral (axillary) bud growth by auxin produced at the apical meristem, promoting vertical growth.

questions.q: When a stem is exposed to light from only one direction, how does auxin redistribute?
opts: It moves to the illuminated side.
It moves to the shady side.
It travels down to the root cap and stops moving.
It is completely broken down by the light.
questions.exp: Under unidirectional light, auxin accumulates on the shady side of the stem, stimulating cell elongation there and causing the stem to bend toward the light.

original_text: Plant Hormones¨Gibberellinsare growth-promoting hormones ¤Gibberellins cause stem elongation; ~70 types nEach differ slightly chemically nMost common -gibberellic acid¤Can be used commercially to grow larger crops, and can be used to break dormancy in plants
explanation: Gibberellins are growth-promoting hormones that primarily stimulate stem elongation. There are approximately 70 chemically distinct types of gibberellins, with gibberellic acid being the most common. In agriculture, gibberellins are used commercially to increase the size of crops and fruits. They are also applied to seeds to break dormancy and initiate germination.

explanation: Cytokinins are plant hormones that promote cytokinesis (cell division) and are found in actively dividing tissues like root tips, seeds, and fruits. The ratio of auxin to cytokinin concentrations determines the differentiation of cells into specific tissues (such as shoots or roots) in tissue cultures. Cytokinins are used to extend the freshness of cut flowers and stored vegetables. Cytokinins and auxins interact to prevent senescence (the aging process). Furthermore, cytokinins can oppose auxin's apical dominance, shifting growth from the terminal bud to lateral axillary buds.

explanation: Abscisic acid (ABA) is synthesized by green plant tissues that contain chloroplasts. Often referred to as the stress hormone, ABA is crucial for survival under unfavorable conditions. It initiates and maintains bud and seed dormancy, preventing premature germination. Germination proceeds when ABA levels decrease and gibberellin levels rise. ABA also protects the plant against water loss during drought by inducing stomatal closure.

original_text: Plant Hormones¨Ethylene(H2C = CH2) is a gas formed from the amino acid methionine. ¨Effects of ethylene ¤AbscissionnEthylene stimulates certain enzymes, such as cellulase, which helps cause leaf, fruit, or flower drop ¤Ripening of fruits nIncreases the activity of enzymes, such as cellulase, that soften fruits nPromotes the activity of enzymes that produce the flavor and smell of ripened fruits. ¤Axillary bud inhibition ¤Suppression of stem and root elongation
explanation: Ethylene ($H_2C=CH_2$) is a gaseous plant hormone synthesized from the amino acid methionine. Unlike other plant hormones, ethylene diffuses through the air to coordinate responses. Ethylene promotes abscission (the dropping of leaves, fruits, or flowers) by stimulating enzymes like cellulase to break down cell walls at the drop site. It accelerates fruit ripening by increasing cellulase activity to soften the fruit and promoting other enzymes that generate the characteristic flavor and aroma of ripe fruit. Additionally, ethylene inhibits axillary bud growth and suppresses stem and root elongation.

questions.q: What gaseous plant hormone is derived from the amino acid methionine?
questions.exp: Ethylene is a gaseous hormone ($H_2C=CH_2$) synthesized from the amino acid methionine.

explanation: A tropism is a directional plant growth response toward or away from a unidirectional environmental stimulus. Positive tropism refers to growth toward the stimulus, whereas negative tropism refers to growth away from the stimulus. Major types of tropisms include gravitropism (response to gravity), phototropism (like stems bending toward light), and thigmotropism (growth response to mechanical touch).

questions.q: What is the term for plant growth directed away from a unidirectional stimulus?
questions.exp: Growth away from a stimulus is a negative tropism; growth toward a stimulus is a positive tropism.

questions.q: Which tropism is correctly matched with its stimulus?
questions.exp: Thigmotropism is growth in response to touch, phototropism is in response to light, and gravitropism is in response to gravity.

original_text: Plant Responses¨Gravitropism¤When a plant is placed on its side, the stem grows upward, opposite of the pull of gravity ¤Stems with root caps grow downward ¤Response depends on sensors called statolithsnStatolithsare starch grains in amyloplasts, which due to gravity settle at gravity side of cellnAuxin may be responsible for gravitropism of roots and shoots
explanation: Gravitropism is a plant's growth response to gravity. When a plant is laid horizontally, the stem exhibits negative gravitropism by growing upward, opposite to gravity's pull. Conversely, roots (which require their root caps to sense gravity) exhibit positive gravitropism by growing downward. This gravity-sensing mechanism relies on statoliths, which are heavy starch grains housed within organelles called amyloplasts. Under gravity, statoliths sink to the lower side of the cell, triggering a redistribution of auxin that coordinates the bending response in both roots and shoots.

questions.q: What structures act as gravity sensors in plant cells, and where are they located?
opts: Perforated plates located in vessel elements
questions.exp: Statoliths are dense starch grains located in amyloplasts. They sink to the lower side of the cell to allow gravity perception.

questions.q: What hormone is primarily responsible for coordinating the differential growth seen in gravitropism?

original_text: Plant Responses¨Phototropism ¤Positive phototropism of stems nOccurs because cells on the shady side of the stem elongate due to the presence of auxin nA pigment in the cell membrane (phototropin) absorbs blue light & initiates phototropism¨Thigmotropism¤Unusual growth due to contact with solid objects nCoiling of tendrils ¤Thigmomorphogenesisoccurs when the entire plant responds to the presence of environmental stimuli nWind/Rain
explanation: This slide covers phototropism, thigmotropism, and thigmomorphogenesis. Positive phototropism in stems causes them to bend toward light because auxin accumulates on the shady side of the stem, stimulating cell elongation there. The light signal is detected by phototropin, a blue-light absorbing receptor pigment located in the cell membrane. Thigmotropism is a growth response to contact with solid objects, such as the coiling of tendrils around a support. Thigmomorphogenesis refers to structural changes in the entire plant's growth pattern (such as growing shorter or sturdier) in response to environmental mechanical forces like wind or rain.

questions.q: Which pigment absorbs blue light to initiate phototropism in stems?
questions.exp: Phototropin is a blue-light photoreceptor in the cell membrane that initiates phototropism.

questions.q: What term describes the structural growth response of an entire plant to mechanical forces like wind and rain?
questions.exp: Thigmomorphogenesis is the growth response of an entire plant to mechanical stimuli like wind or rain, whereas thigmotropism is localized growth (like coiling) upon contact.

explanation: Nastic movements (also known as turgor movements) are rapid, reversible plant movements that do not involve growth and are independent of the direction of the stimulus. These movements are driven by rapid changes in turgor pressure as water enters or leaves specialized motor cells. Nastic movements are triggered by stimuli such as touch, shaking, or temperature changes. Classic examples include the folding of leaves in the sensitive plant (Mimosa pudica) and the rapid snap-closure of a Venus flytrap.

questions.exp: Nastic movements are turgor movements driven by rapid, reversible turgor pressure changes as water enters and exits motor cells.

explanation: Sleep movements are daily, rhythmic movements in plants that occur in response to transitions between light and dark. These movements are guided by circadian rhythms, which are endogenous biological rhythms that operate on an approximate 24-hour cycle. Circadian rhythms are persistent and continue even in the absence of external environmental cues, indicating they are controlled by an internal biological clock. These rhythms are closely integrated with photoperiodism (the plant's response to day/night length).

questions.q: What is a key feature of circadian rhythms in plants?
opts: They only occur in response to physical touch.
They operate on a 24-hour cycle and persist even without environmental stimuli.
They are growth responses that cause stems to bend toward blue light.
They require the digestion of insects to function.
questions.exp: Circadian rhythms are 24-hour biological cycles that are self-sustaining and continue even in the absence of external cues, regulated by an internal biological clock.

original_text: Plant Responses¨Photoperiodism¤Any physiological response prompted by changes in day or night length nInfluences flowering in some plants nRequires participation of a biological clock and a plant photoreceptor called phytochrome¤Phytochrome is a blue-green leaf pigment that alternately exists in two forms nPhytochrome red (Pr) is inactivenPhytochrome far-red (Pfr) is active nConversion of forms allows a plant to detect photoperiod changes nAlso promotes seed germination and inhibits stem elongation
explanation: Photoperiodism is any physiological response (such as flowering) prompted by changes in the relative lengths of day and night. This mechanism requires an internal biological clock and the plant photoreceptor pigment phytochrome. Phytochrome is a blue-green leaf pigment that exists in two interconvertible forms: 1) Phytochrome red ($P_r$): the inactive form that absorbs red light. 2) Phytochrome far-red ($P_{fr}$): the active form that absorbs far-red light. The interconversion between these two forms allows the plant to track photoperiodic changes. Active $P_{fr}$ also functions to promote seed germination and inhibit stem elongation.

questions.q: Which pigment acts as the photoreceptor in photoperiodism?
questions.exp: Phytochrome is the leaf pigment that acts as a photoreceptor to detect changes in day and night length.

questions.q: Which form of phytochrome is the active form?
questions.exp: Phytochrome far-red (Pfr) is the physiologically active form, while Phytochrome red (Pr) is inactive.

questions.q: Which of the following is promoted by the active form of phytochrome (Pfr)?
questions.exp: Active phytochrome (Pfr) promotes seed germination and inhibits stem elongation.

explanation: Flowering plants are categorized into three groups based on how photoperiod affects their flowering: 1) Short-day plants: flower when the day length is shorter (meaning the continuous dark period is longer) than a critical threshold. 2) Long-day plants: flower when the day length is longer (continuous dark period is shorter) than a critical threshold. 3) Day-neutral plants: flower independently of day length. Additionally, some plants require a specific sequence of photoperiods to trigger flowering.

They flower only during the summer solstice.
questions.exp: Short-day plants flower when the day length is shorter than a critical length (corresponding to a long night).

questions.q: Which plants are unaffected by day length when it comes to initiating flowering?
questions.exp: Day-neutral plants are not dependent on day length to trigger flowering.

explanation: Plants have evolved diverse physical and chemical defenses to protect themselves from herbivores and parasites. 1) Physical defenses: include the waxy cuticle and tough bark. 2) Chemical defenses: include secondary metabolites like tannins (found in tea), alkaloids (such as morphine, nicotine, and caffeine), and cyanogenic glycosides (which break down into toxic cyanide to inhibit cellular respiration). 3) Wound responses: involve the systemic release of chemicals like systemin and proteinase inhibitors to deter herbivores when tissue is damaged. 4) Hypersensitive response (HR): a localized tissue defense that seals off and isolates infected/wounded areas. 5) Indirect defenses: mechanisms that prevent insects from laying eggs. 6) Mutualisms: such as between the acacia tree and acacia ants.
