original_text: Reproductive Strategies¨Plants have a two-stage, alternating life cycle¤Sporophyteproduces haploid spores by meiosis¤Spores divide mitotically to become haploid gametophytes¤Gametophytes produce gametes¤Gametes fuse to produce a diploid zygote¤Zygote divides mitotically to become the diploid sporophyte
explanation: Plants undergo an alternation of generations, a life cycle that alternates between two multicellular stages: 1) The diploid (2n) sporophyte, which produces haploid (n) spores through meiosis. 2) These spores divide by mitosis to develop into the haploid (n) gametophyte. The gametophyte produces haploid gametes (sperm and egg) by mitosis. During fertilization, these gametes fuse to form a diploid (2n) zygote. The zygote then divides mitotically to grow into the diploid sporophyte, completing the cycle.

explanation: Flowering plants are heterosporous, producing two distinct types of spores: 1) Microspores: male spores that develop in the anther. A microspore undergoes mitosis to become a pollen grain, which is the male gametophyte. 2) Megaspores: female spores that develop in the ovary. A megaspore undergoes mitosis to become the female gametophyte (embryo sac), which is housed inside an ovule within the ovary. After fertilization, the ovule matures into a seed, and the ovary develops into a fruit.

explanation: Flowering is initiated by environmental cues like photoperiod (day length). Monocots and eudicots display differences in floral structure: monocot flower parts are arranged in groups or multiples of three, whereas eudicot flower parts are arranged in groups or multiples of four or five. A typical flower has four whorls of modified leaves attached to the receptacle (the swollen tip of the flower stalk, or peduncle): 1) Sepals: protect the developing flower bud. 2) Petals: attract animal pollinators. 3) Stamens (male organs): consist of a pollen-producing sac (anther) on a slender stalk (filament). 4) Carpels (female organs): consist of a sticky pollen-receptive tip (stigma), a stalk (style), and an base (ovary) that encloses one or more ovules. Fused carpels form a compound carpel, as seen in fruits like oranges.

explanation: Flowers are classified by the presence of their structures: 1) Complete flowers possess all four floral whorls: sepals, petals, stamens, and carpels. Incomplete flowers lack one or more of these structures. 2) Perfect (bisexual) flowers possess both male (stamens) and female (carpels) reproductive organs. Imperfect (unisexual) flowers lack one of the reproductive organs. 3) Monoecious plants bear separate staminate (male) and carpellate (female) flowers on the same individual plant. 4) Dioecious plants bear staminate and carpellate flowers on separate individual plants, meaning that two distinct plants of different sexes are required to achieve pollination and produce fruit.

explanation: This slide describes male and female gametophyte development. 1) Male gametophytes: are produced in the anthers, which contain four pollen sacs. Diploid microspore mother cells in these sacs undergo meiosis to produce haploid microspores, which then undergo mitosis to form pollen grains. 2) Female gametophyte: develops inside the ovary's ovules. The ovule consists of parenchyma cells covered by integuments. One parenchyma cell enlarges to become a diploid megaspore mother cell, which undergoes meiosis to produce four haploid megaspores; three degenerate, leaving one functional megaspore. The functional megaspore undergoes mitosis to produce an 8-nucleate embryo sac containing: one egg cell flanked by two synergid cells, one central cell with two polar nuclei, and three antipodal cells.

original_text: Reproductive Strategies¨Pollination¤The transfer of pollen from an anther to the stigma of a carpelnSelf-pollination occurs if the pollen is from the same plantnCross-pollination occurs if the pollen is from a different plant¨Fertilization¤When a pollen grain lands on the stigma, it germinates, forming a pollen tube¤The pollen tube passes between the stigma and style to reach the micropyle of the ovule¤Double fertilization occursnOne sperm nucleus unites with the egg nucleus, producing a 2n zygotenThe other sperm nucleus unites with the polar nuclei, forming a 3n endosperm nucleus, which develops into the endosperm¤A mature seed contains the embryo, stored food, and the seed coat
explanation: Pollination is the transfer of pollen from the anther to the stigma of a carpel. It can be self-pollination (same plant) or cross-pollination (different plant). Upon pollination, the pollen grain germinates, forming a pollen tube that grows down through the style to reach the ovule's micropyle. Angiosperms undergo double fertilization: one sperm nucleus fuses with the egg cell to form a diploid (2n) zygote (which becomes the embryo). The other sperm nucleus fuses with the two polar nuclei in the central cell, forming a triploid (3n) endosperm nucleus that develops into endosperm tissue to nourish the embryo. The mature seed consists of the embryo, stored food, and a protective seed coat.

questions.q: What is the product of the fusion between the second sperm nucleus and the two polar nuclei during double fertilization?
questions.exp: The second sperm nucleus fuses with the two polar nuclei of the central cell to produce a triploid (3n) endosperm nucleus, which develops into nutrient storage tissue.

questions.q: What is the term for the path that sperm nuclei travel through the style to reach the micropyle of the ovule?
questions.exp: The pollen grain germinates on the stigma to form a pollen tube, which grows through the style to reach the micropyle of the ovule.

explanation: Development is a programmed series of structural and functional changes from simple to complex forms. In eudicot seeds, following double fertilization, the diploid zygote undergoes repeated cell division to form two structures: the proembryo (which will develop into the plant embryo) and the suspensor (which anchors the embryo and transfers nutrients to it).

questions.q: In eudicot seed development, what two structures are directly formed by the division of the zygote?
questions.exp: The zygote divides repeatedly to form a proembryo (the precursor to the embryo) and a suspensor.

original_text: Seed Development¨During the globular stage, the proembryois a ball of cells¤The outermost cells will become dermal tissue¨Heart and Torpedo Stages¤The embryo is heart shaped when cotyledonsappear¤The embryo enlarges, elongates, and takes on a torpedo shape¨Mature Embryo¤The epicotylis the portion between cotyledons contributing to shoot development¤The hypocotylis the portion below that contributes to stem development¤The radicleis the embryonic root
explanation: The developing eudicot embryo transitions through several stages: 1) Globular stage: the proembryo is a ball of cells, and its outer layer is destined to differentiate into dermal tissue. 2) Heart stage: the embryo becomes heart-shaped as two cotyledons emerge. 3) Torpedo stage: the embryo enlarges and elongates. 4) Mature embryo: exhibits defined structures: the epicotyl (the region above cotyledon attachment that develops into the shoot), the hypocotyl (the region below cotyledon attachment that contributes to stem development), and the radicle (the embryonic root).

questions.q: Which embryonic region is responsible for developing into the root of the plant?
questions.exp: The radicle is the embryonic root of the plant.

questions.q: What is the developmental sequence of stages for a eudicot embryo?
questions.exp: The embryo develops from a globular stage (ball of cells) to a heart stage (cotyledons appear), then elongates into a torpedo shape, and finally becomes a mature embryo.

questions.q: What will the outermost cells of the globular stage proembryo become?
questions.exp: During the globular stage, the outermost cells of the proembryo are determined to develop into dermal tissue.

original_text: Seed Development¨Monocot and eudicot structures differ slightly , especially regarding how nutrients are stored in the seed. ¤In monocots, cotyledon store nutrients and also absorb other molecules from the endospermnSee below, endosperm disappears in the corn kernal¤In eudicots, cotyledon stores all nutrients embryo will need
explanation: Seed structures in monocots and eudicots differ in nutrient storage. In monocot seeds (e.g., corn), the single cotyledon absorbs nutrients from the endosperm and transfers them to the embryo; the endosperm is present during seed development and is absorbed during germination. In eudicot seeds, the two cotyledons absorb all the nutrients from the endosperm during seed development and store them directly, so the mature seed contains no separate endosperm tissue.

questions.q: How is nutrient storage different in eudicot seeds compared to monocot seeds?
opts: Eudicot cotyledons store all the nutrients the embryo needs, whereas monocots rely on the cotyledon absorbing nutrients from a separate endosperm.
Monocot seeds store all nutrients in the hypocotyl, whereas eudicots store them in the radicle.
Eudicot seeds retain a large endosperm at maturity, while monocots lack an endosperm entirely.
Monocot seeds store nutrients in the seed coat, while eudicots store them in the suspensor.
questions.exp: In eudicots, the cotyledons store all the nutrients the embryo will need. In monocots, the cotyledon absorbs nutrients from the endosperm.

original_text: Fruit Types & Seed Dispersal¨A fruitis a mature ovary¨Simple Fruits¤Simple fruits are derived from single ovary with one or several chambers¨Compound fruits develop from several groups of ovaries¤Aggregate FruitsnOvaries are from a single flower one receptaclenBlackberry¤Multiple FruitsnOvaries are from separate flowers clustered togethernPineapple
explanation: A fruit is a mature ovary. Fruits are classified by their development: 1) Simple fruits: derive from a single ovary, which may contain one or several chambers. 2) Compound fruits: develop from multiple ovaries. These include aggregate fruits (multiple ovaries from a single flower on one receptacle, e.g., blackberry) and multiple fruits (ovaries from separate flowers clustered together in an inflorescence, e.g., pineapple).

questions.q: What type of fruit is a blackberry, and how does it develop?
opts: Simple fruit; from a single ovary with one chamber
Aggregate fruit; from multiple ovaries of a single flower on one receptacle
Multiple fruit; from ovaries of separate flowers clustered together
Dehiscent dry fruit; from a dry ovary wall that splits open
questions.exp: A blackberry is an aggregate fruit, developing from multiple ovaries of a single flower sharing a single receptacle.

questions.q: A pineapple develops from ovaries of separate flowers clustered together. It is classified as a:
questions.exp: Multiple fruits develop from the ovaries of several separate flowers clustered closely together.

original_text: Fruit Type & Seed Dispersal¨Fruit Development¤The ovary wall thickens to become the pericarp, which can have three layersnThe exocarpforms the outermost skinnThe mesocarpis the fleshy tissue between the exocarp and the endocarpnThe endocarpis the boundary around the seeds¨Fruit Types¤In dry fruits, the pericarp is paper, leathery, or woody when the fruit is maturenDehiscent -the fruit splits open when ripenLegumesnIndehiscent -the fruit does not split open when ripenGrains
explanation: As fruit develops, the ovary wall thickens into the pericarp. In fleshy fruits, the pericarp has three layers: the exocarp (outer skin), mesocarp (fleshy middle tissue), and endocarp (inner boundary around the seeds). In dry fruits, the pericarp is papery, leathery, or woody at maturity. Dry fruits are subclassified as dehiscent (the fruit splits open when ripe to release seeds, e.g., legumes) or indehiscent (the fruit does not split open, e.g., grains).

questions.q: What are the three layers of the pericarp in a fleshy fruit, starting from the outside?
questions.exp: The pericarp consists of the exocarp (outer skin), mesocarp (middle fleshy layer), and endocarp (inner boundary surrounding the seeds).

questions.q: How do dehiscent dry fruits differ from indehiscent dry fruits?
opts: Dehiscent fruits split open when ripe; indehiscent fruits do not split open.
Dehiscent fruits are fleshy; indehiscent fruits are woody.
Dehiscent fruits develop from compound ovaries; indehiscent from simple ovaries.
Dehiscent fruits are wind-dispersed; indehiscent fruits are animal-dispersed.
questions.exp: Dehiscent dry fruits (like legumes) split open at maturity to release seeds. Indehiscent dry fruits (like grains) do not split open.

original_text: Fruit Type & Seed Dispersal¨Dispersal of Fruits¤Many dry fruits are dispersed by windnWoolly hairs, plumes, wings¤Many fruits attract animals and provide them with foodnPeaches, cherries, tomatoes
explanation: Seed dispersal is crucial for plant reproduction. Many dry fruits utilize wind dispersal, possessing structures like wings, plumes, or woolly hairs. Other fruits are fleshy (e.g., peaches, cherries, and tomatoes) and contain nutrients that attract animals, which consume the fruit and disperse the seeds.

questions.q: Which structures are common adaptations for wind dispersal of dry fruits?
questions.exp: Dry fruits adapted for wind dispersal often possess structures such as woolly hairs, plumes, or wings to catch the wind.

original_text: Fruit Type & Seed Dispersal¨Seed Germination¤When seed germination occurs, the embryo resumes growth and metabolic activity¤Length of time seeds retain their viability is quite variable¤Some seeds do not germinateuntil they have been through a dormantperiodnTemperate zones -Cold WeathernFor some, cannot germinate until fruit removed due to inhibitors¨Environmental requirements for seed germination¤Availability of oxygen for metabolic needs¤Adequate temperature for enzyme activity¤Adequate moisture for hydration of cells
explanation: Seed germination is the resumption of embryonic growth and metabolic activity. Seed viability is variable. Many seeds require a dormant period to prevent premature germination: in temperate zones, seeds may require cold exposure, while others cannot germinate until chemical inhibitors in the surrounding fruit are removed. Germination requires three environmental conditions: 1) Oxygen (for cellular respiration), 2) Adequate temperature (for enzyme activity), and 3) Adequate moisture (for cell hydration).

questions.q: What are the three essential environmental conditions required for seed germination?
opts: Carbon dioxide, light, and soil nutrients
Oxygen, adequate temperature, and adequate moisture
questions.exp: Germination requires oxygen for respiration, an adequate temperature for enzymes, and moisture to hydrate the cells.

questions.q: Why do some seeds fail to germinate until their fruit is removed?
opts: The fruit blocks oxygen from reaching the seed coat.
The fruit tissue contains chemical growth inhibitors.
The seeds require mechanical abrasion by wind.
The fruit is too heavy for the radicle to emerge.
questions.exp: For some seeds, chemical growth inhibitors present in the fruit prevent germination until the fruit tissue is removed.

original_text: Asexual Reproduction Strategies¨Vegetative reproduction is any form of asexual reproduction occurring in plants in which a new plant grows from a fragment of the parent plant or a specialized reproductive structure. ¤Many plants naturally reproduce this way, but it can also be induced artificially.¨Plants can reproduce asexually with the use of:¤Stolons–horizontal stems¤Rhizomes –underground stems¨Cutting, grafting, mound layering, & aerial layering are some commonnatural vegetative methods
explanation: Vegetative reproduction is a natural or artificially induced form of asexual reproduction in plants, where a new individual grows from a fragment of the parent plant or from a specialized vegetative structure rather than seeds or spores. Natural asexual structures include stolons (above-ground horizontal stems) and rhizomes (underground horizontal stems). Horticulturalists can artificially propagate plants using common vegetative methods such as cutting, grafting, mound layering, and aerial layering.

questions.q: What is vegetative reproduction in plants?
opts: Reproduction via double fertilization of ovules
Asexual reproduction where a new plant grows from a fragment or vegetative structure of the parent
Growth of a haploid plantlet from cultured anthers
Production of spores by the diploid sporophyte
questions.exp: Vegetative reproduction is a form of asexual reproduction in which new plants develop from vegetative parts of the parent plant (like stems or leaves).

questions.q: Which of the following are specialized stem structures used by plants to propagate asexually?
questions.exp: Stolons (horizontal above-ground stems) and rhizomes (horizontal underground stems) are specialized stems used for vegetative reproduction.

questions.q: Which of the following is an artificial or horticultural vegetative propagation method listed in the text?
questions.exp: Grafting, cutting, mound layering, and aerial layering are listed as common vegetative propagation methods.

original_text: Artificial Reproduction Strategies¨In addition to more natural, horticulture methods of vegetative propagation, there are also some other lab-based methods¨Tissue culture is the growth of a tissue in an artificial liquid or solid culture medium¤Many plant cells are totipotentnEach has the genetic capability of becoming an entire plantnPlants can be genetically modified and then grown in these conditions¨Somatic embryogenesis¤Hormones stimulate development of plantlets from leaf or other tissue¤Tomato, rice, celery, asparagus, lilies, and others developed using this method¨Somaclonalvariations¤Mutations leading to new plants with desirable traits can be selected for and then shipped
explanation: Advanced laboratories utilize biotechnology for plant propagation. 1) Tissue culture is the sterile growth of plant tissue in an artificial liquid or solid culture medium. This relies on the fact that many plant cells are totipotent, meaning each cell possesses the genetic capacity to differentiate and grow into a complete plant. This property allows researchers to grow genetically modified plants from single cells. 2) Somatic embryogenesis: uses plant hormones to stimulate the formation of plantlets directly from somatic tissues, like leaf fragments (used for tomato, rice, celery, asparagus, and lilies). 3) Somaclonal variations: are mutations that spontaneously arise during tissue culture, allowing scientists to select for and propagate plants with new, desirable traits.

questions.q: What does the term 'totipotent' mean in the context of plant cell biology?
opts: The cell can only undergo meiosis to produce spores.
The cell contains chloroplasts and can perform photosynthesis.
The cell has the genetic potential to develop into an entire plant.
The cell is impermeable to water and gases.
questions.exp: Totipotent cells contain the complete genetic program required to regenerate all tissues and develop into a whole, mature plant.

questions.q: What is somatic embryogenesis?
opts: The fusion of male and female gametes in an ovule
Hormonal stimulation of plantlet development from leaf or other non-reproductive tissue
The natural splitting of dry fruits at maturity
Spontaneous mutation occurring in cell suspension cultures
questions.exp: Somatic embryogenesis involves using plant hormones to induce the development of plantlets directly from somatic (vegetative) tissues like leaves.

questions.q: What are somaclonal variations?
opts: Spontaneously occurring mutations in tissue culture that can lead to desirable traits
Modified roots that tap into host plant xylem
Concentric rings of secondary growth in woody stems
Seasonal changes in the opening of stomata
questions.exp: Somaclonal variations are mutations that occur during tissue culture. These variations can be selected by breeders to develop new plants with desirable traits.

original_text: Artificial Reproduction Strategies¨Meristem tissue¤Results in clonal plants with identical traits¨Anther tissue culture¤Haploid cells in pollen grains are cultured to produce haploid plantlets¤A diploid plantlet can be produced by adding a chemical agent that encourages chromosome doubling¨Cell Suspension Culture¤Rapidly growing calluses are cut into small pieces and shaken into a liquid nutrient mediumnSingle cells or small clumps break off and form a suspensionnUsed to extract chemicals and metabolites, many times which have been genetically modified, from plant cells.
explanation: This slide describes three specialized tissue culture techniques: 1) Meristem culture: uses virus-free apical meristem tissue to produce clonal plants with identical genetic traits. 2) Anther tissue culture: involves culturing the haploid cells inside pollen grains to produce haploid plantlets. To make these plants fertile and diploid, scientists add a chemical agent that encourages chromosome doubling. 3) Cell suspension culture: involves taking rapidly growing cell masses (calluses), cutting them into small pieces, and shaking them in a liquid nutrient medium. Single cells or small clumps break off to form a suspension, which is used to extract valuable chemicals and metabolic products, often from genetically modified plant cells.

questions.q: During anther culture, how can a fertile diploid plantlet be generated from haploid pollen cells?
opts: By performing double fertilization in a test tube
By adding a chemical agent that encourages chromosome doubling in haploid plantlets
By grafting the haploid stem onto a diploid rootstock
By growing the plantlets in a medium rich in Rhizobium bacteria
questions.exp: Anther culture initially produces haploid plantlets. A chemical agent is then applied to encourage chromosome doubling, producing fertile diploid plants.

questions.q: What is the procedure for establishing a cell suspension culture?
opts: Grafting a shoot apical meristem onto a root system in liquid soil
Culturing whole flowers in an anaerobic gas chamber
Shaking pieces of rapidly growing callus tissue in a liquid nutrient medium to break off single cells
Extracting seeds and placing them in cold weather to break dormancy
questions.exp: Cell suspension culture is created by cutting calluses into pieces and shaking them in a liquid nutrient medium, causing single cells or small clumps to break off into suspension.

original_text: Types of Tissues¨Tissues are a collection of specialized cells organized to perform a common function¨4 main categories of tissue:¤Epithelial¤Connective¤Muscular¤Nervous
explanation: A tissue is defined as a collection of specialized cells organized to perform a common physiological function. In animals, tissues are classified into four primary categories: epithelial tissue, connective tissue, muscular tissue, and nervous tissue.

questions.q: What are the four primary categories of animal tissues?
questions.exp: The four main categories of animal tissue are epithelial, connective, muscular, and nervous tissue.

original_text: Types of Tissues¨Epithelial Tissue (epithelium)¤Forms a continuous layer over body surfacesnUsually exposed to an environment on one side, and connected to a basement layer on the othernLines body cavitiesnForms glands¤Epithelial cells may be connected to one another bynTight junctions, Adhesion junctions, or Gap junctions¤Functions of epithelial tissue include:nProtection, Secretion, Absorption, Excretion, Filtration¤3 types of epithelial tissue:nSimple, Stratified, or Glandular
explanation: Epithelial tissue (epithelium) forms continuous sheets of cells that cover body surfaces, line internal cavities, and form glands. Epithelial sheets are polar: one surface is typically exposed to the external environment or an internal cavity, while the opposite surface is attached to a basement membrane. Epithelial cells are secured to one another by intercellular junctions: tight junctions, adhesion junctions, or gap junctions. Epithelial tissue performs several vital functions: protection, secretion, absorption, excretion, and filtration. It is structurally classified into simple, stratified, or glandular epithelia.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a primary function of epithelial tissue?
questions.exp: Epithelial tissue functions in protection, secretion, absorption, excretion, and filtration. Contraction and movement is the function of muscular tissue.

questions.q: What are the three types of junctions that connect epithelial cells together?
opts: Sieve plates, Central canals, and Lacunae
Tight junctions, Adhesion junctions, and Gap junctions
questions.exp: Epithelial cells are connected to each other by tight junctions, adhesion junctions, or gap junctions.

original_text: Types of Tissues¨Simple epithelia –A single layer of cells, all touching basement membrane¨Classified according to cell type:¤Squamous-flattened cells¤Cuboidal–cube-shaped cells¤Columnar–cells resembling columns
explanation: Simple epithelia consist of a single layer of cells, where every cell is in direct contact with the basement membrane. Simple epithelia are classified into three types based on cell shape: 1) Squamous: thin, flattened cells. 2) Cuboidal: cube-shaped cells. 3) Columnar: tall, rectangular cells that resemble columns.

questions.q: What defines a simple epithelium?
opts: Multiple layers of cells where only the bottom layer touches the basement membrane
A single layer of cells where every cell touches the basement membrane
A tissue composed of cells suspended in a liquid matrix
Contractile cells containing actin and myosin filaments
questions.exp: Simple epithelia are characterized by having a single layer of cells, all of which are anchored to the basement membrane.

questions.q: Which cell shape in simple epithelia is correctly matched with its description?
questions.exp: Squamous cells are flattened, cuboidal cells are cube-shaped, and columnar cells resemble columns.

original_text: Types of Tissues¨Glandular Epithelia –secretes a product¤A glandcan be a single epithelial cell or can contain many cells¤Exocrine glandsnSecrete products into ducts or cavities¤Endocrine glandsnSecrete products directly into the bloodstreamnPituitary, thyroid¨Stratified epithelia –Layers of cells ¤Only bottom layer touching basement membraned
explanation: 1) Glandular epithelia are specialized to secrete substances. Glands can be unicellular or multicellular, and are classified into: exocrine glands (which secrete products into ducts or internal cavities) and endocrine glands (which lack ducts and secrete hormones directly into the bloodstream, such as the pituitary and thyroid glands). 2) Stratified epithelia consist of multiple stacked layers of cells, where only the deepest (bottom) cell layer is in contact with the basement membrane.

questions.q: How do endocrine glands differ from exocrine glands?
opts: Endocrine glands secrete products into ducts; exocrine glands secrete directly into the blood.
Endocrine glands secrete products directly into the bloodstream; exocrine glands secrete into ducts or cavities.
Endocrine glands are unicellular; exocrine glands are always multicellular.
Endocrine glands are found in stratified epithelia; exocrine in simple epithelia.
questions.exp: Endocrine glands (e.g., pituitary, thyroid) secrete hormones directly into the bloodstream without ducts, while exocrine glands secrete into ducts or cavities.

questions.q: What is the structural characteristic of stratified epithelia?
opts: A single layer of cells, all touching the basement membrane
Cells embedded in an inorganic salt matrix
Multiple layers of cells, with only the bottom layer touching the basement membrane
questions.exp: Stratified epithelia are composed of multiple layers of cells, where only the bottom-most layer touches the basement membrane.

original_text: Types of Tissues¨Connective Tissue¤Specialized cells¤Ground substance -Noncellular material, fills space¤Protein fibersnCollagen fibers -contain collagen providing strength and flexibilitynReticular fibers –contain thinly branched collagen fibersnElastic fibers –contain elastin¤Categories include nFibrous, Supportive, & Fluid
explanation: Connective tissue binds and supports body parts. It is composed of three elements: specialized cells, an extracellular ground substance (a noncellular material that fills the space between cells), and protein fibers. The three types of protein fibers found in connective tissue matrix are: 1) Collagen fibers: provide structural strength and flexibility. 2) Reticular fibers: contain thin, highly branched collagen fibers that form supportive networks. 3) Elastic fibers: contain the protein elastin, allowing the tissue to stretch and recoil. Connective tissue is divided into three major categories: fibrous, supportive, and fluid.

questions.q: What are the three essential components of connective tissue?
opts: Specialized cells, ground substance, and protein fibers
questions.exp: Connective tissue is characterized by having specialized cells, an extracellular ground substance, and protein fibers.

questions.q: Which type of protein fiber provides stretch and recoil capabilities to connective tissues?
questions.exp: Elastic fibers contain the protein elastin, which allows them to stretch and recoil.

original_text: Types of Tissues¨Fibrous Connective Tissue¨Consist of:¤Fibroblastcells¤A matrix containing collagen and elastic fibers¨Loose fibrous connective tissue¤Allows organs to expand¨Adipose tissue¤Stores energy¤Insulates the body and provides padding¨Dense fibrous connective tissue¤Strong connective tissue¤Tendons –connect muscle to bone¤Ligaments –connect bones to other bones at joints
explanation: Fibrous connective tissues consist of fibroblasts (cells that synthesize the extracellular matrix) and a matrix containing collagen and elastic fibers. 1) Loose fibrous connective tissue: supports epithelia and surrounds organs, allowing organs to expand. 2) Adipose tissue: stores energy, insulates the body against heat loss, and cushions organs. 3) Dense fibrous connective tissue: is a strong tissue containing tightly packed collagen fibers. It forms tendons (which connect muscle to bone) and ligaments (which connect bone to bone at joints).

questions.q: What is the function of fibroblasts in fibrous connective tissue?
opts: They contract to produce voluntary movement.
They synthesize the extracellular matrix containing collagen and elastic fibers.
They carry oxygen in the bloodstream.
They receive and integrate sensory input.
questions.exp: Fibroblasts are the characteristic cells of fibrous connective tissue that produce the fibers and ground substance of the extracellular matrix.

questions.q: What is the difference between a tendon and a ligament?
opts: Tendons connect bone to bone; ligaments connect muscle to bone.
Tendons connect muscle to bone; ligaments connect bone to bone at joints.
Tendons store fat; ligaments contain elastic cartilage.
Tendons line body cavities; ligaments form glands.
questions.exp: Tendons connect skeletal muscles to bones, whereas ligaments connect bones to other bones at joints.

questions.q: Which tissue type is specialized for energy storage, insulation, and protective padding?
questions.exp: Adipose tissue is a specialized connective tissue that stores energy in the form of fat, insulates the body, and provides padding.

original_text: Types of Tissues¨Supportive Connective Tissue¤CartilagenClassified according to type of collagen and elastic fibers found in the matrix (hyaline cartilage, elastic cartilage, fibrocartilage)nCartilage cells lie in small chambers (lacuna) in the matrix¤BonenMatrix is inorganic salts deposited around protein fibersnBone cells are located in lacunaenLacunae arranged in concentric circles within osteons around tiny tubes (central canals)
explanation: Supportive connective tissues provide structural strength and include cartilage and bone. 1) Cartilage: features a solid but flexible matrix. It is classified into hyaline cartilage, elastic cartilage, and fibrocartilage based on the fibers in the matrix. Cartilage cells (chondrocytes) reside in small chambers called lacunae within the matrix. 2) Bone: features a rigid matrix composed of inorganic calcium salts deposited around protein fibers. Bone cells (osteocytes) also reside in lacunae. In compact bone, the lacunae are arranged in concentric circles within structural units called osteons, which surround tiny tubes called central canals containing blood vessels and nerves.

questions.q: What are the small chambers within the cartilage and bone matrix that house the cells?
questions.exp: Lacunae are the small chambers in the matrix of bone and cartilage that house osteocytes and chondrocytes, respectively.

questions.q: In compact bone, how are lacunae organized?
opts: Scattered randomly throughout the ground substance
Arranged in concentric circles within osteons around central canals
Lining the outer epidermal surface of the bone
Embedded in a liquid plasma matrix
questions.exp: In compact bone tissue, lacunae containing bone cells are organized in concentric circles within osteons, centered around central canals.

original_text: Types of Tissues¨Fluid Connective Tissue¤BloodnA connective tissue in which cells are embedded in a liquid matrix (plasma)nRed blood cells –oxygen transportnWhite blood cells –immune responsenPlatelets–involved in the clotting processnFunctionsnTransports nutrients and oxygen to cellsnRemoves carbon dioxide and other wastes¤LymphnA fluid connective tissue located in lymphatic vessels
explanation: Fluid connective tissues contain cells suspended in a liquid matrix. The two types are blood and lymph. 1) Blood: is a fluid connective tissue where the extracellular matrix is a liquid called plasma. The cellular elements include red blood cells (erythrocytes, which transport oxygen), white blood cells (leukocytes, which fight infection), and platelets (cell fragments involved in blood clotting). Blood functions to transport oxygen and nutrients to cells and remove carbon dioxide and metabolic wastes. 2) Lymph: is a fluid connective tissue that flows through lymphatic vessels.

questions.q: What is the liquid matrix of blood tissue?
questions.exp: Plasma is the liquid extracellular matrix of blood in which blood cells and platelets are suspended.

questions.q: Which blood component is correctly paired with its primary function?
questions.exp: Red blood cells transport oxygen, white blood cells handle immune defense, and platelets participate in the clotting process.

original_text: Types of Tissues¨Muscular (Contractile) tissue¤Contractile cells containing actin and myosin filaments¤Cells are called muscle fibers¤Three types of muscle tissue:nSkeletal MusclenVoluntary -Long, striated fibers, multinucleatednSmooth (visceral) MusclenInvoluntary -No striationsnCardiac MusclenStriated, but mostly involuntarynCells are bound to each other by intercalated disksnRelies on pacemaker cells for regular contraction
explanation: Muscular tissue is specialized for contraction and movement. It is composed of cells called muscle fibers, which contain contractile protein filaments made of actin and myosin. There are three types of muscle tissue: 1) Skeletal muscle: voluntary, featuring long, cylindrical, striated (banded) fibers containing multiple nuclei per cell. 2) Smooth (visceral) muscle: involuntary, lacking striations, composed of spindle-shaped cells with a single nucleus; found in the walls of internal organs. 3) Cardiac muscle: found only in the heart. It is striated but involuntary. The cardiac cells are branched, single-nucleated, and joined end-to-end by intercalated disks that facilitate rapid electrical coupling. Cardiac contraction is regulated by specialized pacemaker cells.

questions.q: What contractile filaments are found inside muscle fibers?
questions.exp: Muscle fibers contract using specialized protein filaments called actin and myosin.

questions.q: Which type of muscle tissue is striated, involuntary, and has cells connected by intercalated disks?
questions.exp: Cardiac muscle is striated and involuntary, and its cells are bound together by intercalated disks.

questions.q: What is smooth muscle, and where is it located?
opts: Voluntary striated muscle attached to bones
Involuntary, non-striated muscle found in the walls of internal organs
Striated involuntary muscle found in the heart
A fluid connective tissue located in lymphatic vessels
questions.exp: Smooth (visceral) muscle is involuntary and lacks striations. It is located in the walls of internal organs like the digestive tract.

original_text: Types of Tissues¨Nervous Tissue¤Conducts electrical impulses¤Conveys information from one area to another¤Nervous tissue includes:nNeurons -Transmit information, consist of dendrites,a cell body, and an axonnOutside the brain and spinal cord, fibers bound by connective tissue form nerves.nNeuroglia-Support and nourish neuronsnNeuroglia in brain include Microglia, Astrocytes, Oligodentrocytes¨Nervous system (functions):¤Sensory inputnSensory receptors detect changesnTransmit information to the spinal cord and brain¤Data integrationnSpinal cord and brain integrate datanDecision is made regarding appropriate response¤Motor outputnResponse is transmitted to effector (gland or muscle)nEffector initiates the actual response
explanation: Nervous tissue conducts electrical impulses and conveys information throughout the body. It consists of two cell types: 1) Neurons: the cells that transmit information. A neuron consists of dendrites (which receive signals), a cell body (containing the nucleus), and an axon (which transmits signals away). Outside the brain and spinal cord, bundles of axon fibers bound by connective tissue are called nerves. 2) Neuroglia: supporting cells that protect and nourish neurons (in the brain, these include microglia, astrocytes, and oligodendrocytes). The nervous system functions in three steps: 1) Sensory input: sensory receptors detect internal or external changes and transmit signals to the brain/spinal cord. 2) Data integration: the brain and spinal cord process the data and decide on a response. 3) Motor output: the decision is transmitted to effectors (muscles or glands) to execute the response.

questions.q: What are the three structural parts of a neuron?
questions.exp: A neuron consists of dendrites (receive signals), a cell body, and an axon (transmits signals).

questions.q: What is the role of neuroglia, and what are three examples found in the brain?
opts: They contract to produce movement; skeletal, smooth, cardiac
They support and nourish neurons; microglia, astrocytes, oligodendrocytes
They synthesize collagen matrix; fibroblasts, chondrocytes, osteocytes
They secrete hormones; pituitary, thyroid, adrenal
questions.exp: Neuroglia support and nourish neurons. Brain neuroglia include microglia, astrocytes, and oligodendrocytes.

questions.q: What is the correct sequence of nervous system functions in coordinating a response?
opts: Sensory input -> Data integration -> Motor output
Motor output -> Data integration -> Sensory input
Data integration -> Sensory input -> Motor output
Sensory input -> Motor output -> Data integration
questions.exp: First, sensory input detects changes. Next, data integration processes the information. Finally, motor output transmits the response to an effector.

explanation: 1) An organ consists of two or more tissue types working together to perform a specific function. 2) An organ system is composed of several organs cooperating to perform a general process, such as digestion. 3) The animal body features two main cavities: a) Dorsal cavity (toward the back): containing the cranial cavity (housing the brain) and the vertebral canal (housing the spinal cord). b) Ventral cavity (toward the front): divided into the thoracic cavity (housing the heart and lungs), the abdominal cavity (housing most other internal organs), and the pelvic cavity (housing certain reproductive and excretory organs).

explanation: The integumentary system consists of the skin and its accessory structures (such as hair, nails, and glands). The skin has three primary functions: 1) Protection: it covers and protects underlying tissues from mechanical injury, pathogen entry, and dehydration. 2) Temperature regulation: it helps maintain body temperature. 3) Sensory perception: it contains sensory receptors that detect touch, pressure, temperature, and pain. Anatomically, the skin consists of three layers: the superficial epidermis, the deeper dermis, and the underlying subcutaneous layer (hypodermis).

explanation: This slide details the three layers of the skin: 1) Epidermis: the outermost layer, composed of stratified squamous epithelium. Cells produced at the bottom are pushed outward, accumulate the tough protein keratin (keratinization), die, and eventually slough off. It contains melanocytes that produce the pigment melanin. UV radiation can damage epidermal DNA, causing mutations that lead to skin cancer. 2) Dermis: a deeper, thicker layer composed of fibrous connective tissue rich in collagen and elastic fibers. It contains sensory receptors, nerve fibers, and blood vessels. 3) Subcutaneous layer (hypodermis): located beneath the dermis, composed of loose connective tissue.

explanation: Human skin contains several accessory structures: 1) Nails: grow from the nail root and provide a protective covering for the distal ends of fingers and toes. explanation: Homeostasis is the ability of an organism to maintain a relatively constant internal environment despite changes in the outer environment. Different organ systems cooperate to maintain homeostasis: 1) Digestive system: processes food to supply nutrient molecules. 2) Respiratory system: absorbs oxygen and excretes carbon dioxide. 3) Liver and kidneys: store excess glucose as glycogen (regulated by the hormone insulin) and break it down when blood glucose levels fall. 4) Kidneys: excrete metabolic wastes, excess water, and salts under hormonal control.

explanation: Homeostasis is partially controlled by endocrine hormones and is ultimately regulated by the nervous system. The primary homeostatic mechanism is negative feedback, which keeps physiological variables close to a specific set value. A negative feedback loop has two key steps: 1) A sensor detects a change in the internal or external environment. 2) A regulatory center processes this input and initiates an action to reverse the deviation, returning conditions to normal.

explanation: Positive feedback is a mechanism that amplifies a physiological change in the same direction, driving the variable further away from the set point. Unlike negative feedback, positive feedback does not result in equilibrium. It occurs less frequently and regulates rapid, terminal processes. Examples include: 1) Childbirth (uterine contractions stimulate oxytocin, causing stronger contractions). 2) Blood clotting (platelet aggregation recruits more platelets). 3) Protein digestion in the stomach (enzyme activation stimulates more enzyme production). Positive feedback can occasionally be harmful, such as a runaway high fever.

questions.exp: Childbirth, blood clotting, and protein digestion in the stomach are classic examples of positive feedback loops.

original_text: Transport in Invertebrates¨Circulatory System¤Functions to move fluid between various parts of the body¨Small aquatic animals with no circulatory system¤Each cell is expose to water and can independently exchange gases and eliminate wastes¨Pseudocoelomates¤Use a fluid-filled body cavity as a means of transporting substances¨Coelomate echinoderms¤May still rely on body fluids for the purpose of locomotion
explanation: A circulatory system functions to transport fluids and substances between different areas of the body. In contrast, small aquatic animals (like flatworms) lack a circulatory system because every cell is exposed to the water, allowing independent gas exchange and waste elimination via diffusion. Pseudocoelomates (like roundworms) use their fluid-filled body cavity (pseudocoelom) to distribute substances. Coelomate echinoderms (like sea stars) lack a traditional heart and vessels, relying on coelomic fluid for internal transport and locomotion (via the water vascular system).

questions.q: Why do small aquatic animals not require a circulatory system?
opts: They use active transport to move substances through the phloem.
Each cell is directly exposed to water and can independently exchange gases and wastes.
They rely entirely on pseudocoelom fluid for locomotion.
They have high rates of transpiration.
questions.exp: Small aquatic animals have a high surface area-to-volume ratio, meaning each cell is close enough to the environment to perform gas exchange and waste elimination by diffusion without a circulatory system.

questions.q: How do pseudocoelomate animals transport materials throughout their bodies?
opts: Through a system of closed arteries and veins
By pumping hemolymph into open tissue sinuses
By moving fluid through a water vascular system for locomotion
questions.exp: Pseudocoelomates lack blood vessels and instead use their fluid-filled body cavity (pseudocoelom) to transport nutrients and wastes.

original_text: Transport in Invertebrates¨Invertebrates with a Circulatory System¤Two types of circulatory fluids:nBlood-contained within blood vesselsnHemolymph–mixture of blood and tissue fluid that fills the body cavity and surrounds internal organs¤Open Circulatory SystemnHeart pumps hemolymph via vesselsnVessels empty into tissue spaces¤Closed Circulatory SystemnHeart pumps blood to capillariesnGases and materials diffuse to and from nearby cellsnVessels return blood to heart without contact between blood and tissues
explanation: Invertebrates with a circulatory system utilize one of two circulatory fluids: 1) Blood: contained entirely within blood vessels. 2) Hemolymph: a mixture of blood and interstitial fluid that fills the body cavity (hemocoel) and bathes internal organs. Circulatory systems are classified as: 1) Open circulatory systems: where a heart pumps hemolymph through vessels that empty into open tissue spaces, bathing organs directly. 2) Closed circulatory systems: where a heart pumps blood through vessels to capillaries, where gas and nutrient exchange occurs by diffusion, and vessels return the blood directly to the heart without it contacting tissues directly.

questions.q: What is hemolymph?
opts: A fluid that contains only red blood cells
A mixture of blood and tissue fluid that directly bathes internal organs
The inorganic matrix of supportive bone tissue
The liquid that flows through the sieve tube elements of phloem
questions.exp: Hemolymph is a combination of blood and tissue fluid that fills the body cavity and surrounds organs in animals with open circulatory systems.

questions.q: In which type of circulatory system does the heart pump blood to capillaries, where diffusion occurs, and vessels return the blood to the heart without it leaving the vessels?
questions.exp: In a closed circulatory system, blood is confined to vessels and capillaries, and returns to the heart without spilling into body cavities.

original_text: Transport in Vertebrates¨All vertebrates have a closed circulatory system called a cardiovascular system¤Vertebrate heart:nAtria of heart receive blood from general circulationnVentricles of heart pump blood out through blood vessels¤Vertebrate vessels:nArteries-Carry blood away from heartnThicker walls, to accommodate sudden influxes of blood from pump (high pressure)nArterioles–Lead to capillariesnCapillaries-Exchange materials with tissue fluidnAll cells within 60-80um of capillary bednOnly 5% of organisms capillary beds open at one timenVenules-Lead to veinsnVeins-Return blood to heartnThinner walls than arteries (lower blood pressure). Have valves
explanation: All vertebrates possess a closed circulatory system known as a cardiovascular system. The vertebrate heart consists of atria (which receive blood returning from circulation) and ventricles (which pump blood out). Vertebrate vessels include: 1) Arteries: carry blood away from the heart, possessing thick walls to handle the high pressure of pumped blood. 2) Arterioles: branches that lead to capillaries. 3) Capillaries: microscopic vessels where nutrient and gas exchange occurs; cells are within 60-80 $\mu m$ of a capillary bed, and only 5% of beds are open at one time. 4) Venules: collect blood from capillaries and lead to veins. 5) Veins: return blood to the heart, possessing thinner walls (due to lower pressure) and internal valves to prevent backflow.

questions.q: Why do arteries have thicker walls than veins?
opts: To allow for the passive diffusion of oxygen across their walls
To accommodate the high pressure and sudden influxes of pumped blood
To prevent the backflow of low-pressure blood
To store excess glucose as glycogen
questions.exp: Arteries must withstand the high pressure and surges of blood ejected directly from the heart, requiring thicker, more elastic walls than veins.

questions.q: What type of blood vessel is thin-walled and facilitates the exchange of materials, and how close are cells to them?
questions.exp: Capillaries are the sites of material exchange. All cells in the vertebrate body are located within 60-80 micrometers of a capillary bed.

questions.q: What structural feature in veins helps return low-pressure blood to the heart against gravity?
questions.exp: Veins contain one-way internal valves that prevent the backflow of blood, assisting its return to the heart under low pressure.

original_text: Transport in Vertebrates¨Comparison of Circulatory Pathways¤Fish -Blood flows in single loopnSingle atrium and single ventricle¤Amphibians -Blood flows in double loopnSystemic circuit and pulmonary circuitnTwo atria with a single ventricle¤Other vertebrates -Blood flows in a double loopnHeart divided by septum into separate sides
explanation: Vertebrate circulatory pathways vary: 1) Fish: have a single-loop pathway, where blood is pumped from a single ventricle to the gills, then to body tissues, and back to a single atrium. 2) Amphibians: have a double-loop pathway (systemic and pulmonary circuits) and a three-chambered heart with two atria and a single ventricle, which leads to some blood mixing. 3) Other vertebrates (birds and mammals): have a double-loop pathway and a four-chambered heart fully divided by a septum into separate left and right sides, preventing blood mixing.

opts: Double loop; two atria and a single ventricle
Single loop; single atrium and single ventricle
Double loop; heart divided by a septum
questions.exp: Fish possess a single-loop circulatory pathway powered by a two-chambered heart consisting of one atrium and one ventricle.

questions.q: How does the heart of an amphibian differ from that of a mammal?
opts: Amphibians have a two-chambered heart, while mammals have a three-chambered heart.
Amphibians have a three-chambered heart (two atria, one ventricle) with some blood mixing, whereas mammals have a four-chambered heart divided by a septum.
Amphibians have a closed system, while mammals have an open system.
Amphibians have only a systemic circuit, while mammals have only a pulmonary circuit.
questions.exp: Amphibians have a three-chambered heart with two atria and a single ventricle, which allows oxygenated and deoxygenated blood to mix. Mammals have a four-chambered heart divided by a septum, keeping the blood streams separate.

explanation: The human heart is a fist-sized, cone-shaped organ composed of cardiac muscle fibers. It is enclosed in a double-walled membranous sac called the pericardium, which reduces friction during contraction. The heart is located in the thoracic cavity between the lungs, directly behind the sternum, and is tilted so that its pointed apex is oriented toward the left side of the body.

original_text: The Human Cardiovascular System¨Structure of the Heart¤Septumseparates the heart into left & right sides¤Each side has two chambersnUpper two chambers are the atrianThin-wallednReceive blood from circulationnLower two chambers are the ventriclesnThick-wallednPump blood away from heart
explanation: The human heart is divided internally into left and right halves by a muscular wall called the septum. This complete separation prevents oxygenated and deoxygenated blood from mixing. The heart has four chambers: two upper atria and two lower ventricles. The atria are thin-walled because they only receive blood from systemic or pulmonary circulation and pump it a short distance into the ventricles. The ventricles are thick-walled because they must generate enough pressure to pump blood away from the heart to the lungs or the rest of the body.

questions.q: What is the function of the septum in the human heart?
opts: It regulates the rhythm of the heart as a pacemaker.
It separates the heart into left and right sides to prevent blood mixing.
It connects the atria directly to the aorta.
It acts as a valve to prevent backflow into the ventricles.
questions.exp: The septum is a muscular wall that completely separates the left and right sides of the heart, preventing oxygen-poor and oxygen-rich blood from mixing.

questions.q: Why are the walls of the ventricles thicker than the walls of the atria?
opts: The ventricles receive blood from the veins, which is under high pressure.
The ventricles must generate high pressure to pump blood out of the heart, whereas the atria only receive blood.
The ventricles contain pacemaker cells that require thick muscle fibers to generate electrical signals.
The ventricles are exposed to the external thoracic cavity.
questions.exp: Ventricles are thick-walled because they pump blood away from the heart into long vascular pathways under high pressure, while atria are thin-walled as they only receive blood.

original_text: The Human Cardiovascular System¨Structure of the Heart¤Valves open and close to control blood flow through heart –prevents backflownAtrioventricular valvesnTricuspid(3 flap) valve between right atrium and ventriclenBicuspid (2 flap) valve between left atrium and ventriclenSemilunar valvesnPulmonary semilunar valve between right ventricle and pulmonary trunknAortic semilunar valve between left ventricle and aorta
explanation: To ensure one-way blood flow and prevent backflow, the human heart contains four valves that open and close in response to pressure changes. 1) Atrioventricular (AV) valves: separate the atria from the ventricles. The tricuspid valve (three flaps) is located on the right side of the heart, and the bicuspid (mitral, two flaps) valve is on the left side. 2) Semilunar valves: guard the exits of the ventricles. The pulmonary semilunar valve controls blood flow between the right ventricle and the pulmonary trunk, and the aortic semilunar valve controls blood flow between the left ventricle and the aorta.

questions.q: Which valve is located between the right atrium and the right ventricle?
questions.exp: The tricuspid (3-flap) valve is the atrioventricular valve located between the right atrium and the right ventricle.

questions.q: What is the location of the aortic semilunar valve?
opts: Between the right atrium and right ventricle
Between the left atrium and left ventricle
Between the right ventricle and the pulmonary trunk
Between the left ventricle and the aorta
questions.exp: The aortic semilunar valve is located at the exit of the left ventricle, separating it from the aorta.

original_text: The Human Cardiovascular System¨Path of Blood Through Heart¤Blood returning to heart from systemic circuit (O2Poor)nVenae cavae(superior and inferior) return blood to the right atriumnRight atrium pumps blood through the tricuspid valve to right ventriclenRight ventricle pumps blood through the pulmonary semilunar valve to the pulmonary circuit (Lungs)¤Blood returning to heart from pulmonary circuit (O2Rich)nEnters left atriumnLeft atrium pumps blood through the bicuspid valve to the left ventriclenLeft ventricle pumps blood through the aortic semilunar valve to the systemic circuitnBlood pressure greater in aorta¤Oxygen-poor blood never mixes with oxygen-rich blood (in humans)
explanation: In humans, oxygen-poor and oxygen-rich blood never mix. 1) Oxygen-poor blood returning from body tissues via the superior and inferior venae cavae enters the right atrium. The right atrium pumps it through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle, which then pumps it through the pulmonary semilunar valve to the lungs via the pulmonary trunk. 2) Oxygen-rich blood returning from the lungs enters the left atrium. The left atrium pumps it through the bicuspid (mitral) valve into the left ventricle, which then pumps it through the aortic semilunar valve into the aorta to supply the systemic circuit. Blood pressure is significantly higher in the aorta due to systemic resistance.

questions.q: What is the correct pathway of oxygen-poor blood returning to the heart from the body?

Aorta -> Left ventricle -> Aortic semilunar valve -> Left atrium
Venae cavae -> Left atrium -> Tricuspid valve -> Left ventricle -> Aorta
questions.exp: Oxygen-poor blood enters the right side of the heart through the venae cavae, moves to the right atrium, passes the tricuspid valve to the right ventricle, and is pumped past the pulmonary semilunar valve to the lungs.

questions.q: Why is blood pressure highest in the aorta?
opts: It carries deoxygenated blood directly from the veins.
It is fed by the left ventricle, which must contract with high pressure to pump blood through the entire body.
It is under the direct control of the SA node pacemaker cells.
It receives blood directly from the pulmonary veins.
questions.exp: The aorta receives blood from the thick-walled left ventricle, which must generate high pressure to distribute blood to the entire systemic circuit.

original_text: The Human Cardiovascular System¨Heartbeat¤Systole-Contraction of heart chambers¤Diastole-Relaxation of heart chambers¤Cardiac cycle -Two-part pumping action that takes about a secondnBlood collects in atria, the atria contractnPushes blood through tricuspid and mitral valves into the resting lower ventriclesnAtrioleSystole, Ventricular Diastole nSecond part begins after the ventricles fillnVentricles contractnAV valves close, Semilunar valves open “Lubsound”nAtrioleDiastole, Ventricular Systole nAfter blood moves into the pulmonary artery and aorta, the ventricles relaxnSemilunar valves close “Dub sound”
explanation: The heartbeat is regulated by the cardiac cycle, which consists of systole (contraction of heart chambers) and diastole (relaxation of heart chambers). This cycle is a two-part pumping action lasting about one second: 1) Atrial Systole, Ventricular Diastole: Blood collects in the atria, which contract, pushing blood through the tricuspid and mitral (bicuspid) valves into the relaxed ventricles. 2) Atrial Diastole, Ventricular Systole: Once the ventricles fill, they contract. The sudden pressure closes the AV valves (producing the 'lub' sound) and opens the semilunar valves. 3) Ventricular Diastole: As blood enters the pulmonary trunk and aorta, the ventricles relax, and the semilunar valves snap shut to prevent backflow, producing the 'dub' sound.

questions.q: What event is responsible for generating the 'lub' sound of the heartbeat?
opts: The closure of the atrioventricular (AV) valves during ventricular systole
The closure of the semilunar valves during ventricular diastole
The flow of blood through the capillary beds
questions.exp: The first heart sound ('lub') is caused by the snapping shut of the atrioventricular (tricuspid and mitral) valves when the ventricles contract during ventricular systole.

questions.q: What occurs during the second part of the cardiac cycle when the ventricles contract?
opts: Closure of the semilunar valves and opening of the AV valves
Both atria and ventricles relax simultaneously
questions.exp: When the ventricles contract (ventricular systole), the atria are relaxed (atrial diastole).

questions.q: What causes the 'dub' sound of the heartbeat?
opts: The opening of the AV valves
The closing of the semilunar valves during ventricular diastole
The passage of blood through the venae cavae
The electrical charging of the SA node
questions.exp: The second heart sound ('dub') is produced by the closure of the semilunar valves as the ventricles relax.

original_text: The Human Cardiovascular System¨Heartbeat¤Pulseis a wave effect passing down the walls of the arterial blood vessels when the aorta expands and recoils falling ventricular systole¤Rhythmic contraction of the heart is due to the cardiac conduction systemnSinoatrial node (SA) keeps the heartbeat regular (pacemaker)nAtrioventricular node (AV) signals ventricles to contract¨Electrocardiogram (ECG)¤A recording of electrical changes that occur in the myocardium during cardiac cycle¤When SA node triggers an impulse, atrial fibers produce an electrical charge (P wave)nP wave indicates the atria are about to contract¤QRS complex signals that the ventricles are about to contract and the atria are relaxing¤T wave is due to electrical changes occurring as the ventricular muscle fibers recover
explanation: This slide discusses the electrical control of the heart. 1) Pulse: a pressure wave traveling along arterial walls as the aorta expands and recoils following ventricular systole. 2) Conduction system: the rhythmic contraction of the heart is driven by the cardiac conduction system. The Sinoatrial (SA) node acts as the pacemaker, initiating the impulse and keeping the rhythm regular. The Atrioventricular (AV) node delays the signal before sending it to stimulate ventricular contraction. 3) Electrocardiogram (ECG): records electrical changes in the heart muscle (myocardium). explanation: Respiration refers to all the physiological events that result in gas exchange between an organism's cells and the environment. All gas exchange occurs passively via diffusion. The process consists of three main steps: 1) Ventilation (breathing): involving inspiration (inhalation of air into the lungs) and expiration (exhalation of air out of the lungs). 2) External Respiration: the exchange of gases between air in the alveoli and blood in the pulmonary capillaries. 3) Internal Respiration: the exchange of gases between systemic capillaries and the surrounding tissue fluid. explanation: Gas exchange in water requires more energy than in air because water is denser and contains far less dissolved oxygen. Consequently, active fish expend up to 25% of their energy on respiration, compared to only 1–2% for humans. Simple, small aquatic animals (like hydra and planarians) have a high surface-area-to-volume ratio, allowing direct diffusion between cells and the environment. Small terrestrial invertebrates, such as earthworms, use their moist body surface for gas exchange, bringing capillaries close to the skin to facilitate diffusion.

explanation: Gills are highly vascularized respiratory organs used by aquatic animals to extract dissolved oxygen from water. Gills maximize efficiency using countercurrent exchange, where water flows in the opposite direction to the flow of oxygen-depleted blood in the capillaries. This maintains a concentration gradient along the entire contact length, allowing gills to extract up to 90% of the oxygen from the water. If a concurrent system (same direction) were used, oxygen concentration would rapidly reach equilibrium, halting diffusion.

explanation: Insects have an open circulatory system, where hemolymph is contained within the open hemocoel cavity, making it inefficient for gas transport. Air sacs act as bellows, inflating and deflating to pump air through the tracheal tubes.

explanation: The human respiratory tract conducts air through a continuous pathway: nose, pharynx, trachea, bronchi, and lungs. The larynx (voice box) and trachea (windpipe) are held open by rigid cartilage rings to facilitate air movement. During swallowing: 1) the larynx rises, 2) the epiglottis covers the glottis (the opening to the larynx) to block food entry, and 3) the soft palate moves backward to cover the entrance to the nasal passages.

explanation: Mammals breathe using negative pressure ventilation. During inspiration (inhalation): 1) the diaphragm contracts and moves downward, and 2) the intercostal muscles contract, elevating the rib cage. These actions expand the volume of the thoracic cavity, causing the air pressure inside the lungs to decrease below atmospheric pressure. The higher atmospheric pressure outside then forces air into the lungs.

explanation: All terrestrial vertebrates, except birds, utilize tidal ventilation for breathing. In this mechanism, air moves in and out along the same route. Because of this, the lungs are not completely emptied and refilled during each cycle. Instead, fresh inhaled air mixes with stale, oxygen-depleted air remaining in the lungs. Tidal ventilation helps conserve water, but it reduces the overall efficiency of gas exchange.

explanation: Birds utilize a highly efficient one-way ventilation mechanism. Because of this one-way flow, fresh inhaled air never mixes with stale, used air, maximizing the concentration gradient and gas-exchange efficiency.

questions.q: What is the pathway of air flow in a bird's respiratory system?
opts: Trachea -> Anterior sacs -> Lungs -> Posterior sacs -> Expelled
Trachea -> Posterior sacs -> Lungs -> Anterior sacs -> Expelled
questions.exp: Air in birds flows from the trachea to the posterior sacs, through the lungs, into the anterior sacs, and is then expelled.

questions.q: Why is bird ventilation more efficient than mammalian ventilation?
opts: Birds perform countercurrent exchange using skin capillaries.
Fresh air never mixes with used air due to one-way flow.
Birds have larger alveoli than mammals.
Birds use positive pressure to inhale air.
questions.exp: One-way flow prevents inhaled air from mixing with stale air, ensuring that the lungs are always supplied with high-oxygen air.

original_text: Breathing and Transport of Gases¨Modifications of Breathing in Humans ¤Normally, adults have a breathing rate of 12 to 20 ventilations per minute ¤The rhythm of ventilation is controlled by a respiratory centerin the medulla oblongata of the brain nSends out impulses to the diaphragm and intercostal muscles of the rib cage so that inspiration occurs nWhen the respiratory center stops sending neuronal signals to the diaphragm and the rib cage, expiration occurs¤Although this center regulates breathing, it can be influenced by nervous or chemical input
explanation: Human adults typically have a resting breathing rate of 12 to 20 ventilations per minute. The rhythm of ventilation is controlled by the respiratory center in the medulla oblongata of the brain. The medulla sends nerve impulses to the diaphragm and intercostal muscles to stimulate contraction, causing inspiration. When these signals stop, the muscles relax, resulting in passive expiration. The respiratory center's activity is modulated by nervous and chemical inputs (such as blood carbon dioxide and pH levels).

questions.q: Which part of the brain controls the automatic rhythm of breathing?
questions.exp: The respiratory center in the medulla oblongata of the brainstem coordinates the rhythmic signals for breathing.

questions.q: What causes passive expiration to occur under the control of the medulla oblongata?
opts: The medulla sends an active signal for the diaphragm to relax.
The medulla stops sending impulses to the diaphragm and intercostal muscles, causing them to relax.
The SA node fires an inhibitory charge.
Carbon dioxide levels drop to zero.
questions.exp: Inspiration is active and driven by nerve impulses. When the medulla stops sending these signals, the muscles relax, causing passive expiration.

original_text: Breathing and Transport of Gases¨Gas Exchange and Transport ¤Partial pressure nThe amount of pressure exerted by a gas nGases diffuse from areas of higher to lower partial pressure ¤Ventilation causes the alveoli to have a higher partial pressure of oxygen and a lower partial pressure of carbon dioxide than the blood in the pulmonary capillaries nThis accounts for the exchange of gases in the lungs nThe opposite occurs in the tissues of the body¤Gas Exchange Video
explanation: Gas exchange is driven by differences in partial pressure (the pressure exerted by an individual gas in a mixture). Gases diffuse down their pressure gradient from high to low partial pressure. Ventilation maintains a higher partial pressure of oxygen ($P_{O2}$) and a lower partial pressure of carbon dioxide ($P_{CO2}$) in the alveoli compared to the blood entering the pulmonary capillaries, driving oxygen into the blood and carbon dioxide out. In systemic tissues, the opposite gradient exists, driving oxygen into tissues and carbon dioxide into the blood.

questions.q: What drives the diffusion of gases across respiratory membranes?
opts: Differences in partial pressure, with gases moving from high to low pressure
The movement of cilia in the trachea
The flow of lymph through the thoracic duct
questions.exp: Gases diffuse passively down their partial pressure gradients, moving from areas of higher partial pressure to lower partial pressure.

questions.q: What are the partial pressure conditions in the alveoli relative to the pulmonary capillaries that facilitate gas exchange in the lungs?
opts: Alveoli have lower PO2 and higher PCO2.
Alveoli have higher PO2 and lower PCO2.
Alveoli and capillaries are at exact oxygen equilibrium.
questions.exp: Ventilation keeps alveolar PO2 high and PCO2 low, allowing oxygen to diffuse into the low-oxygen blood and carbon dioxide to diffuse out of the high-CO2 blood.

original_text: Breathing and Transport of Gases¨Transport of Oxygen and Carbon Dioxide ¤External Respiration nOxygen (O2)from alveoli combine with hemoglobin (Hb) in RBC to form oxyhemoglobin (HbO2)¤Internal Respiration nOxyhemoglobin (HbO2)gives up oxygen, which diffuses out of the blood into the tissues where it is taken up by cells nSome carbon dioxide (CO2) enters blood from tissues and binds with hemoglobin to form carbaminohemoglobin (HbCO2)nMost carbon dioxide is transported in the form of bicarbonate ion (HCO3-)
explanation: Oxygen and carbon dioxide are transported chemically in the blood. 1) External respiration: In the lungs, oxygen diffuses into RBCs and binds to hemoglobin (Hb) to form oxyhemoglobin ($HbO_2$). 2) Internal respiration: In systemic tissues, oxyhemoglobin ($HbO_2$) dissociates to release oxygen, which diffuses into cells. Carbon dioxide ($CO_2$) diffuses from tissues into the blood. Some $CO_2$ binds to hemoglobin, forming carbaminohemoglobin ($HbCO_2$), but most carbon dioxide is converted and transported as bicarbonate ions ($HCO_3^-$) in the plasma.

questions.q: What is formed when oxygen binds to hemoglobin in the lungs?
questions.exp: In the lungs, oxygen combines with hemoglobin (Hb) to form oxyhemoglobin (HbO2).

questions.q: In what chemical form is the majority of carbon dioxide transported in the blood?
questions.exp: While some CO2 binds to hemoglobin as carbaminohemoglobin, the vast majority is converted into bicarbonate ions (HCO3-) for transport in plasma.

explanation: This slide contrasts two common disorders of the upper respiratory tract. 1) Common Cold: a mild viral infection presenting with sneezing, a runny nose, and mild fever. Because it is viral, antibiotics are ineffective. 2) Strep Throat: acute pharyngitis (inflammation of the pharynx) caused by the bacterium Streptococcus pyogenes. Symptoms include a severe sore throat, high fever, and swollen tonsils. Since it is bacterial, it is treatable and curable with antibiotics.

questions.q: Why are antibiotics ineffective in treating a common cold?

original_text: Respiration and Human Health¨Disorders of the Lower Respiratory Tract¤Trachea and Bronchi nChoking nAcute bronchitis nInfection of primary and secondary bronchi nChronic bronchitis nAirways become inflamed and filled with mucus nAsthma nAirways are unusually sensitive to specific irritants nWhen exposed to these irritants, smooth muscles in the bronchioles undergo spasms
explanation: Lower respiratory tract disorders affecting the trachea and bronchi include: 1) Choking: mechanical blockage of the windpipe. 2) Acute bronchitis: a temporary infection of the primary and secondary bronchi. 3) Chronic bronchitis: a long-term condition where the bronchial airways become inflamed and filled with excess mucus. 4) Asthma: a disease where the airways are hypersensitive to specific irritants (like pollen or dust). Exposure to these triggers spasms in the smooth muscles of the bronchioles, causing constriction and breathing difficulty.

questions.q: What happens in the bronchioles during an asthma attack?
opts: The smooth muscles in the bronchioles undergo spasms and constrict the airways.
Alveoli fill with fluid and burst.
Fibrous connective tissue builds up around the trachea.

questions.q: How does chronic bronchitis differ from acute bronchitis?

Chronic bronchitis involves long-term airway inflammation and mucus buildup, whereas acute bronchitis is a temporary infection of the bronchi.
Chronic bronchitis causes the epiglottis to fail, while acute bronchitis affects the lungs.
Chronic bronchitis is treated with bronchiole spasms, while acute bronchitis is treated with a bellows system.

original_text: Respiration and Human Health¨Disorders Affecting the Lungs ¤Pneumonia nViral, bacterial, or fungal infection of the lungs in which bronchi and alveoli fill with fluid ¤Pulmonary tuberculosis nCaused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis nResults in lung damage and reduced function ¤Pulmonary fibrosis nFibrous connective tissue builds up in the lungs¤Emphysema nAlveoli are distended and walls are damaged, reducing the surface area available for gas exchange ¤Lung Cancer nBegins with thickening and callusing of the cells lining the airways nAtypical cells appear in the thickened lining nCells from the tumor break loose and metastasize
explanation: This slide details major lung disorders: 1) Pneumonia: a viral, bacterial, or fungal infection where the bronchi and alveoli fill with fluid. 2) Pulmonary tuberculosis: caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, resulting in significant lung damage. 3) Pulmonary fibrosis: a buildup of fibrous connective tissue that reduces lung elasticity. 4) Emphysema: a disease where alveoli become distended and their walls are damaged, reducing the surface area for gas exchange. 5) Lung Cancer: begins with the thickening of airway linings, followed by the appearance of atypical cells and tumor formation, which can metastasize.

questions.q: Which lung disease is characterized by the destruction of alveolar walls and reduced gas-exchange surface area?

questions.exp: Pneumonia is an infection of the lungs that causes the bronchi and alveoli to fill with fluid, compromising gas exchange.

questions.exp: Pulmonary tuberculosis is caused by the bacterium Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

original_text: Evolution of the Nervous System¨Invertebrate Nervous System Organization¤HydrasnNerve net composed of neurons in contact with one anothernAlso in contact with contractile cells in the body wall¤PlanariansnLadderlike nervous systemnCephalization-a concentration of ganglia and sensory receptors in the head¤Annelids, Arthropods and MolluscsnComplex animalsnTrue nervous systems
explanation: Invertebrate nervous system organization varies by complexity: 1) Hydras (cnidarians) have a simple nerve net of interconnected neurons in contact with contractile cells in the body wall, lacking a brain. 2) Planarians (flatworms) have a ladderlike nervous system with longitudinal cords and exhibit cephalization (the concentration of ganglia and sensory receptors in the head). 3) Annelids, arthropods, and molluscs are more complex invertebrates that possess true nervous systems.

questions.q: What type of nervous organization is characteristic of hydras?

The concentration of ganglia and sensory receptors in the head; planarians

questions.exp: Cephalization is the evolutionary trend toward concentrating nervous tissue and sensory receptors at the anterior (head) end, seen in planarians.

original_text: Evolution of the Nervous System¨Vertebrate Nervous System Organization¤Central nervous systemnDevelops from an embryonic dorsal neural tubenCephalization and bilateral symmetry result in several paired sensory receptorsnEyes, ears, olfactory structures¤Vertebrate brain is organized into three areasnHindbrainnMidbrainnForebrain
explanation: The vertebrate nervous system is characterized by a central nervous system (CNS) that develops from an embryonic dorsal neural tube. Bilateral symmetry and cephalization result in paired sensory receptors located in the head (eyes, ears, and olfactory structures). The vertebrate brain is structurally organized into three primary regions: the hindbrain, midbrain, and forebrain.

questions.q: From what embryonic structure does the vertebrate central nervous system develop?

questions.q: What are the three evolutionary divisions of the vertebrate brain?

original_text: Evolution of the Nervous System¨Division of Nervous System:¤The Central Nervous System (CNS)nIncludes the brain and spinal cord¤The Peripheral Nervous System (PNS)nConsists of all nerves and ganglia that lie outside the CNSnTwo divisionsnSomatic nervous systemnSensory and motor functions that control skeletal musclenAutonomic nervous systemnControls smooth muscle, cardiac, muscle, and glandnDivided into sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions
explanation: The nervous system is divided into: 1) The Central Nervous System (CNS): consisting of the brain and spinal cord. 2) The Peripheral Nervous System (PNS): consisting of nerves and ganglia outside the CNS. The PNS has two divisions: a) Somatic nervous system: handles sensory and motor functions controlling voluntary skeletal muscle. b) Autonomic nervous system: controls involuntary smooth muscle, cardiac muscle, and glands, and is subdivided into the sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions.

questions.q: What structures compose the Central Nervous System (CNS)?

questions.exp: The CNS is made up of the brain and the spinal cord.

questions.q: What are the two subdivisions of the autonomic nervous system?
questions.exp: The autonomic system is split into the sympathetic ('fight or flight') and parasympathetic ('rest and digest') divisions.
