original_text: Nervous Tissue¨Neurons(Nerve Cells)¤Cell body contains nucleus and organelles¤Dendritesreceive signals from sensory receptors or other neurons¤Axonconducts nerve impulses to another neuron or to other cellsnCovered by myelin sheathnAny long axon is also called a nerve fiber¨Types of Neurons¤Motor (efferent) neuronsnAccept nerve impulses from the CNSnTransmit them to muscles or glands¤Sensory (afferent) neuronsnAccept impulses from sensory receptorsnTransmit them to the CNS¤InterneuronsnConvey nerve impulses between various parts of the CNS
explanation: Nervous tissue is composed of neurons (nerve cells). Neurons consist of: 1) Cell body: containing the nucleus and organelles. 2) Dendrites: receive incoming signals. 3) Axon: conducts impulses away; long axons are covered in myelin and are called nerve fibers. Neurons are functionally divided into: 1) Sensory (afferent) neurons: carry impulses from receptors to the CNS. 2) Interneurons: convey signals between parts of the CNS. 3) Motor (efferent) neurons: carry impulses from the CNS to effector muscles or glands.

questions.q: What are the three structural parts of a neuron?
questions.exp: A neuron consists of a central cell body, signal-receiving dendrites, and a signal-conducting axon.

questions.q: Which type of neuron transmits impulses from sensory receptors to the Central Nervous System?
questions.exp: Sensory (afferent) neurons carry sensory information from peripheral receptors toward the central nervous system.

questions.q: What is the term for a long axon?
questions.exp: Any long axon is also referred to as a nerve fiber.

original_text: Nervous Tissue¨Transmission of Nerve Impulses ¤Resting PotentialnThe membrane potential (voltage) when the axon is not conducting an impulsenThe inside of a neuron is more negative than the outside, around -70 mVnDue in part to the activity of the sodium-potassium pump¤An action potential is a rapid change in polarity across a portion of an axonal membranenAn action potential is generated only after a stimulus larger than the thresholdnGated channel proteinsnOne channel protein suddenly allows sodium to enter the cellnAnother channel protein allows potassium to leave the cell
explanation: Nerve impulses are electrical signals. 1) Resting Potential: the voltage across the axonal membrane when it is not conducting an impulse, typically around -70 millivolts ($mV$) with the inside being more negative. This polarization is maintained in part by the active transport of the sodium-potassium pump. 2) Action Potential: a rapid, temporary polarity reversal across the axonal membrane. It is generated only if a stimulus exceeds a specific threshold. During an action potential, gated channels open sequentially: sodium ($Na^+$) channels open, allowing sodium to enter the cell (depolarization), followed by potassium ($K^+$) channels opening, allowing potassium to exit (repolarization).

questions.q: What is the resting membrane potential of a neuron, and how is it characterized?
opts: Around +35 mV; inside is more positive
Around -70 mV; inside is more negative
Around 0 mV; inside and outside are equal
Around -120 mV; inside has no charge
questions.exp: The resting membrane potential of a neuron is about -70 mV, with the interior of the axon being electrically negative relative to the extracellular fluid.

questions.q: What ion movement is responsible for the initial depolarization phase of an action potential?
opts: Calcium ions entering the synaptic cleft
questions.exp: Depolarization occurs when gated channel proteins open and allow sodium (Na+) to enter the cell, reversing the membrane's electrical charge.

original_text: Nervous Tissue¨Propagation of Action Potentials¤In nonmyelinated axons, the action potential travels down an axon one small section at a time¤In myelinated fibers, an action potential at one node causes an action potential at the next nodenSaltatory (jumping) Conduction¤Conduction of a nerve impulse is an all-or-nothing eventnIntensity of signal is determined by how many impulses are generated within a given time span¨Once an action potential has moved on, the previous section goes through a refractory period, where Na+channels are unable to open¨Action Potential Short Video
explanation: Action potential propagation depends on axon myelination: 1) Nonmyelinated axons: the action potential travels continuously, depolarizing one small adjacent section at a time. 2) Myelinated axons: the action potential jumps from one node to the next, a process called saltatory (jumping) conduction. 3) General principles: Conduction is an all-or-nothing event. Signal intensity is determined by the frequency of impulses (how many are generated per unit time), not the size of the potential. As the impulse propagates, the preceding membrane segment undergoes a refractory period during which its sodium ($Na^+$) channels are inactivated, preventing backward propagation.

questions.q: What is saltatory conduction?
opts: The movement of sodium through the sodium-potassium pump
The jumping of an action potential from node to node along a myelinated axon
The continuous depolarization of a nonmyelinated axon
The release of neurotransmitters into the synaptic cleft
questions.exp: Saltatory conduction is the rapid, jumping propagation of action potentials along myelinated axons from one node of Ranvier to the next.

questions.q: Why does an action potential only propagate in one direction down an axon?
opts: The myelin sheath blocks backward flow.
The previous section of axon is in a refractory period where its sodium channels cannot open.
Dendrites actively repel incoming electrical charges.
The sodium-potassium pump only runs in one direction.
questions.exp: During the refractory period, sodium channels are temporarily inactivated, ensuring that the action potential cannot travel back toward the cell body.

original_text: Nervous Tissue¨Transmission Across a Synapse¤A synapse is a region where neurons nearly touch¤Small gap between neurons is the synaptic cleft¤Transmission across a synapse is carried out by neurotransmittersnSudden rise in calcium in the axon terminal of one neuronnCalcium stimulates synaptic vesicles to merge with the presynaptic membranenNeurotransmitter molecules are released into the synaptic cleft¨Synaptic Integration¤A single neuron is on the receiving end ofnMany excitatory signals, andnMany inhibitory signals¤IntegrationnThe summing of excitatory and inhibitory signalsnThe receiving dendrite must receive enough + or –signal to cross a threshold and continue propagating action potentialSynapse Video Clip
explanation: A synapse is the region where neurons nearly touch, separated by a small gap called the synaptic cleft. Transmission is mediated by chemical neurotransmitters: when an action potential reaches the axon terminal, calcium ($Ca^{2+}$) channels open, and the influx of calcium stimulates synaptic vesicles to fuse with the presynaptic membrane, releasing neurotransmitters into the cleft. A postsynaptic neuron receives many excitatory and inhibitory signals. Synaptic integration is the summing of these inputs. The postsynaptic neuron will only fire an action potential if the integrated net signal crosses the threshold.

questions.q: What ion triggers the release of neurotransmitters from synaptic vesicles at the presynaptic membrane?
questions.exp: An action potential arriving at the axon terminal triggers an influx of calcium ions, which signals synaptic vesicles to fuse with the membrane and release neurotransmitters.

questions.q: What is synaptic integration?
opts: The myelination of the axon to increase signal speed
The mathematical summing of excitatory and inhibitory signals by a receiving neuron
The fusion of the axon terminal with the postsynaptic dendrite
The recycling of neurotransmitters by the glial cells
questions.exp: Synaptic integration is the process by which a neuron sums all the excitatory and inhibitory inputs it receives to determine if it will generate an action potential.

original_text: The Central Nervous System¨Consists of the brain and spinal cord¤Three specific functions:nReceives sensory inputnPerforms integrationnGenerates motor output¤Spinal cord and brain are wrapped in three protective membranes called meningesnSpaces between meninges are filled with cerebrospinal fluidnFluid is continuous with that of central canal of spinal cord and the ventriclesof the brain
explanation: The Central Nervous System (CNS) consists of the brain and spinal cord, performing three primary functions: receiving sensory input, integrating information, and generating motor output. The brain and spinal cord are wrapped in three protective membranes called meninges. The spaces between the meninges are filled with cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), which cushions the CNS. This fluid is continuous with the fluid in the central canal of the spinal cord and the ventricles of the brain.

questions.q: What are the three protective membranes that surround the brain and spinal cord?
questions.exp: The meninges are the three layers of protective membranes wrapping the brain and spinal cord.

questions.q: Where is cerebrospinal fluid located, and what is its path of continuity?
opts: Only in the heart cavities, continuous with blood plasma
Between the meninges, continuous with the central canal of the spinal cord and the brain ventricles
In the pleural space, continuous with lymphatic capillaries
Within the synovial joints, continuous with the bursa
questions.exp: Cerebrospinal fluid fills the spaces between the meninges and is continuous with the fluid in the spinal cord's central canal and the brain's ventricles.

original_text: The Central Nervous System¨The Spinal Cord¤Two main functionsnCenter for many reflex actionsnMeans of communication between the brain and spinal nerves¤Composed of grey matter and white matternCell bodies and short unmyelinated fibers give the gray mater its colornMyelinated long fibers of interneurons running in tracts give white mater its color
explanation: The spinal cord has two primary functions: it serves as the center for many reflex actions, and it is the pathway of communication between the brain and spinal nerves. It is composed of gray matter and white matter. Gray matter (located centrally) contains neuronal cell bodies and short, unmyelinated fibers. White matter (located peripherally) contains tracts of long, myelinated interneuron fibers that carry signals up and down the spinal cord.

questions.q: What are the two primary functions of the spinal cord?
opts: Pumping blood and filtering metabolic wastes
Serving as a reflex center and communicating between the brain and spinal nerves
Releasing insulin and storing glucose as glycogen
Performing external respiration and filtering inhaled air
questions.exp: The spinal cord acts as the integration center for reflexes and provides a pathway of communication between the brain and peripheral spinal nerves.

questions.q: What gives white matter in the spinal cord its characteristic color?
opts: Myelinated long fibers of interneurons running in tracts
Cell bodies and short, unmyelinated fibers
A dense network of lymphatic capillaries
questions.exp: The lipid-rich myelin sheaths wrapping the long interneuron axons running in tracts give white matter its white appearance.

original_text: The Central Nervous System¨The Brain¤The cerebrumis the largest portion of the brain in humansnCommunicates with, and coordinates the activities of, the other parts of the brainnLongitudinal fissure divides the cerebrum into left and right cerebral hemispheres¤Cerebral CortexnA thin but highly convoluted outer layer of gray matternCovers the cerebral hemispheresnContains motor areas and sensory areas as well as association areasnPrimary motor area is in the frontal lobe, just ventral to the central sulcusnPrimary somatosensory area is in the parietal lobe, just dorsal to the central sulcusnBasal nucleinIntegrate motor commandsnEnsures that the proper muscle groups are either activated or inhibited
explanation: The cerebrum is the largest portion of the human brain, divided by the longitudinal fissure into left and right hemispheres. The cerebral cortex is the thin, highly folded (convoluted) outer layer of gray matter covering these hemispheres. It contains motor, sensory, and association areas: 1) The primary motor area is in the frontal lobe, ventral (anterior) to the central sulcus. 2) The primary somatosensory area is in the parietal lobe, dorsal (posterior) to the central sulcus. 3) Basal nuclei are deep gray matter masses that integrate motor commands, activating or inhibiting muscle groups to coordinate movement.

questions.q: What deep groove divides the cerebrum into left and right hemispheres?
questions.exp: The longitudinal fissure is the deep cleft that divides the cerebrum into left and right hemispheres.

questions.q: Where are the primary motor and primary somatosensory areas located in the cerebral cortex?
opts: Primary motor is in the parietal lobe; primary somatosensory is in the frontal lobe.
Primary motor is in the frontal lobe; primary somatosensory is in the parietal lobe.
Both are located in the occipital lobe.
Primary motor is in the pons; primary somatosensory is in the medulla.
questions.exp: The primary motor area is situated in the frontal lobe (ventral to the central sulcus), and the primary somatosensory area is in the parietal lobe (dorsal to the central sulcus).

questions.q: What is the function of the basal nuclei?
opts: They secrete melatonin to regulate sleep cycles.
They integrate motor commands to ensure proper muscle activation or inhibition.
They act as the primary relay station for olfactory signals.
They generate the reflex centers for sneezing and coughing.
questions.exp: Basal nuclei integrate motor commands from the cortex to ensure smooth, coordinated movement by activating or inhibiting specific muscle groups.

original_text: The Central Nervous System¨Other Parts of the Brain¤DiencephalonnA region encircling the third ventriclenIncludes three structuresnHypothalamusnForms the floor of the third ventriclenIntegrating center that maintains homeostasisnControls the pituitary glandnThalamusnConsists of two masses of gray matter located in the sides and roof of the third ventriclenReceives all sensory input except smellnIntegrates sensory information and sends it to the cerebrumnPineal glandnSecretes melatonin
explanation: The diencephalon encircles the third ventricle of the brain and contains three structures: 1) Hypothalamus: forms the floor of the third ventricle. It is the main integrating center for maintaining homeostasis (regulating variables like temperature, hunger, and water balance) and controls the pituitary gland. 2) Thalamus: consists of two gray matter masses in the sides and roof of the third ventricle. It receives all sensory inputs (except smell), integrates them, and relays them to the cerebrum. 3) Pineal gland: secretes the hormone melatonin, which regulates circadian sleep-wake cycles.

questions.q: Which part of the diencephalon acts as the homeostatic integrating center and controls the pituitary gland?
questions.exp: The hypothalamus forms the floor of the third ventricle and serves as the main homeostatic control center, regulating the pituitary gland.

questions.q: What sensory input bypasses the thalamus?
questions.exp: The thalamus receives and integrates all sensory input except for smell (olfaction) before sending it to the cerebrum.

questions.q: What is the function of the pineal gland?
opts: It secretes insulin to store glycogen.
It secretes melatonin to regulate sleep cycles.
It secretes acetylcholine to slow the heart rate.
It secretes sebum to lubricate hair follicles.
questions.exp: The pineal gland secretes melatonin, a hormone involved in regulating sleep-wake cycles.

original_text: The Central Nervous System¨Other Parts of the Brain¤Brain StemnContains the midbrain, pons, and the medulla oblongatanMidbrainnActs as a relay station for tracts passing between the cerebrum and the spinal cord or cerebellumnPonsnContains axons that form a bridge between the cerebellum and the rest of the central nervous systemnMedulla OblongatanContains reflex centers for vomiting, coughing, sneezing, hiccupping, and swallowing
explanation: The brain stem connects the higher brain regions with the spinal cord and consists of three structures: 1) Midbrain: acts as a relay station for nerve tracts passing between the cerebrum and the spinal cord or cerebellum. 2) Pons: contains bundles of axons that form a bridge between the cerebellum and the rest of the central nervous system. 3) Medulla oblongata: contains vital reflex centers for coughing, sneezing, vomiting, hiccupping, and swallowing, in addition to cardiovascular and respiratory centers.

questions.q: Which part of the brain stem contains reflex centers for swallowing, sneezing, and vomiting?
questions.exp: The medulla oblongata contains reflex centers that regulate coughing, sneezing, vomiting, hiccupping, and swallowing.

questions.q: What is the function of the pons?
opts: It acts as the primary pacemaker of the heart.
It contains axons that form a bridge between the cerebellum and the rest of the CNS.
It processes and stores long-term memories.
It secretes melatonin to control sleep cycles.
questions.exp: The pons (meaning 'bridge') contains axons that route signals between the cerebellum and the rest of the nervous system.

original_text: The Central Nervous System¨The Reticular Activating System (RAS)¤A complex network of:nNuclei (masses of gray matter)nNerve fibers that extend the length of the brain stem¤The reticular formation is a major component of the RAS¤The RAS arouses the cerebrum via the thalamus and causes a person to be alert¨Limbic System¤Complex network of tracts and “nuclei”¤Incorporates the medial portions of the cerebral lobes, the basal nuclei, and the diencephalon¤Integrates higher mental functions and primitive emotions¤Important structures in the limbic system are the hippocampusand the amygdala
explanation: This slide describes two major functional networks: 1) Reticular Activating System (RAS): a network of gray matter nuclei and nerve fibers running through the brain stem. Its major component is the reticular formation. The RAS filters sensory input and arouses the cerebrum via the thalamus, causing alertness and maintaining consciousness. 2) Limbic System: a network of tracts and nuclei incorporating parts of the cerebral lobes, basal nuclei, and diencephalon. It integrates higher mental functions (learning/reasoning) with primitive emotions (fear, anger, pleasure). Two key limbic structures are the hippocampus (memory) and the amygdala (emotion).

questions.q: What is the primary function of the Reticular Activating System (RAS)?
opts: It controls the secretions of the pituitary gland.
It arouses the cerebrum via the thalamus to maintain alertness and consciousness.
It serves as a pathway for reflex arcs in the spinal cord.
It coordinates the five tastes on the tongue.
questions.exp: The RAS is responsible for filtering sensory information and triggering cortical arousal, keeping a person alert and awake.

questions.q: Which system integrates higher mental functions and primitive emotions, and what are two of its key structures?
opts: Autonomic system; sympathetic and parasympathetic nerves
Tracheal system; trachea and air sacs
questions.exp: The limbic system integrates higher cognitive functions with emotional states, and contains the hippocampus and the amygdala.

original_text: The Central Nervous System¨Learning and Memory¤MemorynThe ability to hold a thought in mind or recall events from the past¤LearningnTakes place when we retain and use past memories¤Short term memory is associated with the prefrontal area of the frontal lobe¤Long term memory is associated with the hippocampus
explanation: Memory is the cognitive ability to hold a thought in mind or recall past events, and learning occurs when past memories are retained and applied. Memory is structurally divided: 1) Short-term memory: is associated with the prefrontal area of the frontal lobe. 2) Long-term memory: is processed and stored with the help of the hippocampus.

questions.q: Which brain region is primarily associated with short-term memory?
opts: The prefrontal area of the frontal lobe
questions.exp: Short-term memory processing is localized in the prefrontal cortex of the frontal lobe.

questions.q: What brain structure is critical for long-term memory?
questions.exp: Long-term memory storage and consolidation are heavily dependent on the hippocampus, a structure in the limbic system.

original_text: The Peripheral Nervous System¨Somatic System¤Includes cranial nerves and spinal nervesnGather information from sensors and conduct decisions to effectorsnControls the skeletal muscles¤Voluntary¨Autonomic system¤Controls the smooth muscles, cardiac muscles, and glands¤Innervates all internal organs¤Usually involuntary¤Divided into two divisionsnSympathetic divisionnParasympathetic division¤Utilizes two neurons and one ganglion for each impulse
explanation: The Peripheral Nervous System (PNS) connects the CNS to effectors and receptors. It is divided into: 1) Somatic system: includes cranial and spinal nerves. It gathers sensory inputs and conducts motor decisions to voluntary skeletal muscles. 2) Autonomic system: regulates involuntary activity of smooth muscles, cardiac muscles, and glands, innervating all internal organs. It is divided into the sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions. The autonomic motor pathway is unique because it utilizes a two-neuron relay (preganglionic and postganglionic) and one intervening ganglion to transmit each impulse, unlike the single-neuron somatic pathway.

questions.q: Which division of the PNS controls skeletal muscles voluntarily?
questions.exp: The somatic system is responsible for conducting voluntary motor commands to skeletal muscles.

questions.q: How does the motor pathway of the autonomic system differ from that of the somatic system?
opts: The autonomic system uses a dorsal neural tube.
The autonomic system utilizes a two-neuron pathway and one ganglion for each impulse.
The autonomic system does not use neurotransmitters.
The autonomic system is under voluntary control.
questions.exp: Somatic motor pathways use a single neuron to reach the target muscle, whereas autonomic pathways use two neurons (preganglionic and postganglionic) and synapse within a ganglion.

original_text: The Peripheral Nervous System¨Reflex Arc¤Sensory receptors generate a nerve impulse that moves along sensory axons through a dorsal root ganglion toward the spinal cord¤Sensory neurons pass signals on to many interneurons in the gray matter of the spinal cord¤Nerve pulses travel along motor axons to an effector, which brings about a response to the stimulus
explanation: A reflex arc is the neural pathway that controls an action reflex. The sequence is: 1) Sensory receptors detect a stimulus and generate an impulse. 2) The impulse travels along sensory axons, passing through their cell bodies located in the dorsal root ganglion, to enter the spinal cord. 3) In the spinal cord's gray matter, sensory neurons synapse with and pass signals to interneurons. 4) The interneurons integrate the information and synapse with motor neurons. 5) Impulses travel along motor axons out of the spinal cord to an effector (muscle or gland), producing a rapid response.

questions.q: In a spinal reflex arc, where are the cell bodies of the sensory neurons located?
opts: In the gray matter of the spinal cord
questions.exp: The cell bodies of afferent sensory neurons are housed outside the spinal cord within the dorsal root ganglion.

questions.q: Trace the correct flow of an impulse through a spinal reflex arc.
opts: Sensory receptor -> motor neuron -> interneuron -> sensory neuron -> effector
Sensory receptor -> sensory neuron -> interneuron (gray matter) -> motor neuron -> effector
Effector -> motor neuron -> dorsal root ganglion -> brain -> sensory receptor
Sensory receptor -> dorsal neural tube -> brain stem -> effector
questions.exp: The impulse starts at a receptor, travels along a sensory neuron, passes through an interneuron in the spinal cord gray matter, moves down a motor neuron, and activates the effector.

original_text: The Peripheral Nervous System¨Sympathetic division¤Especially important during fight or flight responses¤Accelerates heartbeat and dilates bronchi¤Norepinephrine main neurotransmitter¨Parasympathetic division¤Promotes all internal responses associated with a relaxed state¤Promotes digestion and retards heartbeat¤Acetylcholine main neurotransmitter
explanation: The autonomic system has two divisions: 1) Sympathetic division: active during stressful 'fight-or-flight' responses. It accelerates heart rate, dilates bronchi (increasing airflow), and inhibits digestion. Its primary postganglionic neurotransmitter is norepinephrine. 2) Parasympathetic division: promotes relaxed 'rest-and-digest' functions. It slows (retards) heart rate and promotes digestion. Its primary postganglionic neurotransmitter is acetylcholine.

questions.q: What division of the autonomic nervous system is active during 'fight-or-flight' responses, and what is its main neurotransmitter?
questions.exp: The sympathetic division triggers 'fight-or-flight' responses using norepinephrine as its primary postganglionic neurotransmitter.

questions.q: Contrast the physiological effects of the sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions.
opts: Sympathetic slows heartbeat and promotes digestion; parasympathetic accelerates heartbeat and dilates bronchi.
Sympathetic accelerates heartbeat and dilates bronchi; parasympathetic slows heartbeat and promotes digestion.
Sympathetic controls skeletal muscle; parasympathetic controls smooth muscle.
Sympathetic uses acetylcholine; parasympathetic uses norepinephrine.
questions.exp: Sympathetic activation prepares the body for action (higher heart rate, open airways); parasympathetic activation promotes rest and digestion (slower heart rate, active digestive system).

Sense Organs Outline
explanation: This slide outlines the subtopics for the Sense Organs section: 1) Sensory Receptors, 2) Chemical Senses, 3) Sense of Vision, 4) Senses of Hearing and Balance, and 5) Somatic Senses.

questions.q: Which of the following is listed in the Sense Organs Outline?
questions.exp: Somatic Senses is the final subtopic listed in the outline for Sense Organs.

original_text: Sensory Receptors¨Sensory receptors¤Specialized cells capable of detecting changes in internal or external conditions, and of communicating that information to the central nervous system¤Capable of facilitating sensory transductionnConversion of an event (stimulus) occurring in the environment into a nerve impulsenThere is no difference between the nerve impulses carried by different types of sensory nervesnPerceptions–Any sensory stimuli of which humans, and perhaps other animals, become conscious¤ChemoreceptorsnSensory receptors responsible for taste and smell¤PhotoreceptorsnSensory receptors responsible for responding to light¤MechanoreceptorsnSensory receptors stimulated by mechanical forces, such as pressure¤ThermoreceptorsnSensory receptors stimulated by changes in temperature
explanation: Sensory receptors are specialized cells that detect environmental changes and transmit this information to the CNS. They perform sensory transduction, converting an environmental stimulus into a nerve impulse. All nerve impulses are identical; sensory differences are determined by the brain pathway. Perceptions are stimuli of which an organism becomes consciously aware. Receptors are classified by stimulus: 1) Chemoreceptors: respond to chemicals (taste/smell). 2) Photoreceptors: respond to light. 3) Mechanoreceptors: respond to mechanical forces (pressure/stretch). 4) Thermoreceptors: respond to temperature changes.

questions.q: What is sensory transduction?
opts: The propagation of an action potential along myelinated axons
The conversion of an environmental stimulus into a nerve impulse by a sensory receptor
The integration of excitatory and inhibitory signals in the dendrites
The fusion of synaptic vesicles with the presynaptic membrane
questions.exp: Sensory transduction is the physiological process where sensory receptors convert physical or chemical environmental stimuli into electrical nerve impulses.

questions.q: If all nerve impulses are identical, how does the brain perceive different sensations like light and sound?
opts: The impulses carry different voltages depending on the stimulus.
The brain interprets sensations based on the specific nerve pathway and cortical region that receives the impulses.
Receptors use different types of neurotransmitters to encode signals.
Different types of action potentials are generated for each sense.
questions.exp: Because all nerve impulses are identical, the brain distinguishes sensory modalities based on the specific nerve pathway and target area of the cerebral cortex where the signals arrive.

questions.q: Match the receptor type with its stimulus: pressure, temperature, chemicals, light.
questions.exp: Chemoreceptors respond to chemicals, photoreceptors to light, mechanoreceptors to mechanical force (pressure), and thermoreceptors to temperature.

original_text: Chemical Senses¨Chemoreception is found almost universally in all animals¤Thought to be the most primitive sense¤Allow organisms to locate food, find a mate, detect dangerous environmental chemicals, etc.¨Sense of Taste in Humans¤In humans, taste buds are located primarily on the tonguenTaste buds open at a taste porenTaste buds have supporting cells and elongated taste cells that end in microvillinFive primary tastesnSweet, sour, salty, bitter, and umami (savory)nTaste buds for each are located throughout the tongue, although certain regions may be more sensitive to particular tastes
explanation: Chemoreception is found in nearly all animals and is considered the most primitive sense, allowing organisms to find food, mates, and avoid toxins. In humans, the sense of taste (gustation) relies on taste buds located primarily on the tongue. Taste buds open at a taste pore and contain supporting cells and elongated taste cells that end in microvilli. There are five primary taste sensations: sweet, sour, salty, bitter, and umami (savory). Taste buds for all five tastes are distributed across the tongue, though specific regions may have higher sensitivity to certain tastes.

questions.q: What are the five primary taste sensations in humans?
opts: Sweet, sour, salty, spicy, and bitter
Sweet, sour, salty, bitter, and umami
Sweet, sour, minty, metallic, and savory
Salty, bitter, acidic, basic, and neutral
questions.exp: The five recognized primary taste sensations in humans are sweet, sour, salty, bitter, and umami (savory).

questions.q: Describe the structure of taste cells within a taste bud.
opts: They are flat squamous epithelial cells that slough off into the taste pore.
They are elongated cells ending in microvilli that project into the taste pore.
They are myelinated axons that contain synaptic vesicles filled with norepinephrine.
They are compound structures composed of thousands of ommatidia.
questions.exp: Taste cells are elongated sensory cells that terminate in microvilli, which project through the taste pore to bind food molecules.

original_text: Chemical Senses¨Sense of Smell in Humans¤Dependent on olfactory cellsnLocated within olfactory epithelium in the roof of the nasal cavity¤Nerve fibers from olfactory cells lead to the same neuron in the olfactory bulb¤Sense of taste and smellnWork together to create a combined effectnInterpreted by the cerebral cortex
explanation: The human sense of smell (olfaction) depends on olfactory cells located in the olfactory epithelium in the roof of the nasal cavity. Nerve fibers from these sensory cells project to the olfactory bulb in the brain, synapsing on shared neurons. The senses of taste and smell function cooperatively, integrating their inputs to produce the perception of flavor, which is processed and interpreted by the cerebral cortex.

questions.q: Where are the sensory cells for smell located in humans?
opts: In the taste buds of the epiglottis
In the olfactory epithelium in the roof of the nasal cavity
In the semicircular canals of the inner ear
In the primary somatosensory area of the parietal lobe
questions.exp: Human olfactory cells are localized in the olfactory epithelium situated in the roof of the nasal cavity.

questions.q: How do taste and smell interact?
opts: They operate entirely independently in different lobes of the brain stem.
They work together to produce a combined flavor effect interpreted by the cerebral cortex.
Smell inhibits taste to prevent overeating.
Taste buds send signals to the olfactory bulb to regulate mucus secretion.
questions.exp: Taste and smell inputs are integrated in the brain to produce a unified sensory perception of flavor, processed in the cerebral cortex.

original_text: Sense of Vision¨How Animals Detect Light¤Photoreceptorsare sensory receptors that are sensitive to light¤ArthropodsnContain compound eyes composed of many independent ommatidianPhotoreceptors generate nerve impulses which pass to the brain by way of optic nerve fibersnInsects have limited color vision, some able to see UV
explanation: Vision depends on photoreceptors, which are sensory receptors sensitive to light. Arthropods (such as insects) possess compound eyes. A compound eye is composed of numerous independent visual units called ommatidia. Photoreceptors within each ommatidium generate nerve impulses in response to light, which travel to the brain via optic nerve fibers. Insects have limited color vision, but some can detect ultraviolet (UV) light.

questions.q: What are compound eyes in arthropods composed of?
opts: A single lens and thousands of retinas
Many independent visual units called ommatidia
questions.exp: Arthropod compound eyes are made of many individual structural and functional units called ommatidia.

questions.q: Which wavelength of light can some insects detect that is invisible to humans?
questions.exp: Many insects can perceive ultraviolet (UV) light, which lies outside the visible spectrum for humans.

original_text: Sense of Vision¨The Human Eye¤Three LayersnSclera-Opaque outer layernFibrous layer covering most of the eyenIn front of the eye, the sclera becomes the transparent corneanConjunctiva–covers surface of the sclera and keeps the eyes moistnChoroid-Thin middle layernContains blood vesselsnIn front of the eye, the choroid thickens to form the ciliary body and the irisnThe iris regulates the size of the pupilnThe lenshelps form imagesnRetina-Inner layernContains photoreceptors called rod cells and cone cellsnContains the fovea centralisnRegion of densely packed cone cells where light is focusednSite where optic nerve connects to the eye creates a blind spot, as no receptors are present
explanation: The human eye consists of three concentric layers: 1) Sclera: the opaque, white outer fibrous layer protecting the eye. At the front, it becomes the transparent cornea, which refracts light. The conjunctiva covers the sclera and keeps the eye moist. 2) Choroid: the thin, vascular middle layer. At the front, it thickens into the ciliary body (controlling lens shape) and the colored iris. The iris regulates pupil size to control light entry, and the lens focuses light to form images. 3) Retina: the innermost layer containing rod cells (low-light vision) and cone cells (color and detail). The fovea centralis is a specialized, cone-dense retinal region where light is focused for maximum sharpness. The site where the optic nerve exits the retina lacks photoreceptors, creating a blind spot.

questions.q: What transparent structure does the sclera become at the front of the eye?
questions.exp: The outer white sclera transitions into the transparent, light-refracting cornea at the front of the eye.

questions.q: What is the function of the iris?
opts: It contains rods and cones to detect light.
It regulates the size of the pupil to control light entry.
It changes the shape of the lens during accommodation.
It moistens the outer surface of the cornea.
questions.exp: The iris is a muscular ring that controls the diameter of the pupil, regulating how much light enters the eye.

questions.q: Why is there a blind spot in the human eye?
opts: Because the cornea is opaque in that region
Because the optic nerve connects to the retina at this point, leaving no space for photoreceptors
Because the fovea centralis contains only blue cones
Because the lens cannot focus light on the ciliary body
questions.exp: The blind spot occurs where ganglion cell axons bundle to form the optic nerve and exit the eye, meaning no rods or cones are present in that specific area.

original_text: Sense of Vision¨Focusing of the Eye¤Light rays pass through the pupil and are focused on the retina¤Focusing starts at the cornea and continues as rays pass through the lens, which provides visual accommodationnShape of lens is controlled by the ciliary musclenDistant object –ciliary muscle is relaxednNear object –ciliary muscle is contracted
explanation: Light rays pass through the pupil and are focused on the retina. Refraction begins at the cornea and continues as the rays pass through the lens, which performs visual accommodation (adjusting shape to focus on objects at different distances). The lens's shape is controlled by the ciliary muscle: 1) for distant objects, the ciliary muscle relaxes, flattening the lens; 2) for near objects, the ciliary muscle contracts, rounding the lens.

questions.q: What muscle controls the shape of the lens for visual accommodation?
questions.exp: The ciliary muscle, a ring of smooth muscle in the ciliary body, controls the shape and curvature of the lens.

questions.q: What is the state of the ciliary muscle when focusing on a near object?
opts: It is relaxed, causing the lens to flatten.
It is contracted, causing the lens to become rounder.
It is completely inactivated by the sympathetic division.
It is undergoing rapid spasms like in asthma.
questions.exp: Focusing on near objects requires the ciliary muscle to contract, allowing the lens to become more rounded and increase its refractive power.

original_text: Sense of Vision¨Photoreceptors of the Eye¤Both rods and cones have an outer segment joined to an inner segment by a stalk¤Pigment molecules are embedded in membrane of the disks in the outer segmentnRhodopsin-pigment composed of opsin and retinal, a derivative of vitamin A¤Rods permit vision in low lightnPeripheral vision and motion¤Cones permit vision in bright lightnFine detail and colornThree different types of cones, each containing a different type of photopigmentnB (blue), G (green), R (red)
explanation: The retina contains rods and cones, which have outer segments with pigment-embedded disks joined to inner segments by a stalk. 1) Rod cells: contain the pigment rhodopsin (opsin protein + vitamin A derivative retinal). Rods permit vision in low light, peripheral vision, and motion detection. 2) Cone cells: operate in bright light to provide high-acuity color vision and fine detail. There are three types of cones, each containing a photopigment sensitive to a different wavelength: Blue (B), Green (G), or Red (R).

questions.q: What are the components of the rod photopigment rhodopsin?
opts: Opsin protein and retinal (a vitamin A derivative)
questions.exp: Rhodopsin is made of the protein opsin bound to retinal, which is derived from vitamin A.

questions.q: Which photoreceptor cell type is responsible for color vision and fine detail in bright light?
questions.exp: Cone cells provide sharp, detailed color vision in bright light conditions.

questions.q: What are the three types of cone cells found in the human eye?
questions.exp: Human color vision is trichromatic, relying on Blue (B), Green (G), and Red (R) cones.

original_text: Sense of Vision¨Integration of Visual Signals in the Retina¤The retina has three layers of neuronsnLayer closest to choroid contains rod and cone cellsnMiddle layer contains bipolar cellsnInnermost layer contains ganglion cells¤Rod and cone cells synapse with the bipolar cells, which in turn synapse with ganglion cells responsible for initiating nerve impulses¤Human retina has approximatelyn150 million rod cellsn6 million cone cellsn1 million ganglion cells¤Since more rod cells synapse on a ganglion cell than cone cells, cone cells provide sharper more detailed images of an object than rod cells
explanation: The retina has three layers of neurons: 1) the photoreceptor layer (rods/cones, closest to the choroid), 2) the middle bipolar cell layer, and 3) the innermost ganglion cell layer. Rods and cones synapse with bipolar cells, which synapse with ganglion cells (whose axons form the optic nerve). The human retina contains roughly 150 million rods, 6 million cones, and 1 million ganglion cells. Because multiple rods converge onto a single ganglion cell, they are sensitive but lack detail. Conversely, fewer cones synapse per ganglion cell (low convergence), meaning cones provide much sharper, more detailed images.

questions.q: What is the pathway of visual signals through the three neuronal layers of the retina?
opts: Ganglion cells -> Bipolar cells -> Rods and cones
Rods and cones (photoreceptors) -> Bipolar cells -> Ganglion cells
Bipolar cells -> Ganglion cells -> Rods and cones
Rods and cones -> Ganglion cells -> Bipolar cells
questions.exp: Light activates photoreceptors (rods and cones), which synapse with bipolar cells, which then synapse with ganglion cells to carry the signal to the brain.

questions.q: Why do cones provide sharper and more detailed images than rods?
opts: Cones contain rhodopsin, which is highly sensitive.
Fewer cone cells synapse on a single ganglion cell compared to rods, leading to less signal convergence.
Cones are located in the blind spot.
Cones use saltatory conduction along their axons.
questions.exp: Rods exhibit high convergence onto ganglion cells, which pools light signals but sacrifices resolution. Cones have low convergence, keeping their spatial signal separate for high detail.

original_text: Senses of Hearing and Balance¨How Animals Detect Sound Waves¤InsectsnTympanum –a membrane stimulated to vibrate by sound waves that directly activates nerve impulses in attached receptor cells¤FishnLateral line system –detects water currents and pressure waves from nearby objects, helping the organism guide their movement and locate other fish
explanation: Animals utilize different adaptations to detect vibrations and pressure changes: 1) Insects: use a tympanum, a thin membrane that vibrates in response to sound waves, directly triggering nerve impulses in attached receptor cells. 2) Fish: use a lateral line system running along the sides of the body to detect water currents and low-frequency pressure waves. This helps them navigate, school, and locate nearby fish.

questions.q: What is the tympanum in insects?
opts: A compound eye unit for UV vision
A vibrating membrane that detects sound waves
A chemoreceptor pore on the antenna
A jointed appendage used for locomotion
questions.exp: The tympanum is a specialized acoustic membrane in insects that vibrates when struck by sound waves, activating auditory receptors.

questions.q: What is the function of the lateral line system in fish?
opts: It detects water currents and pressure waves from nearby objects.
It acts as a brain stem reflex center.
questions.exp: The lateral line system contains mechanoreceptors that detect changes in water currents and pressure waves, aiding navigation and schooling.

original_text: Senses of Hearing and Balance¨The Human Ear¤Outer ear -Pinna and auditory canal¤Middle ear begins at tympanic membrane and ends at ovaland round windowsnThe ossicles(three small bones) are found between the tympanic membrane and the windowsnMalleus(hammer), incus(anvil), and stapes(stirrup)nAuditory tube (eustachian tube) extends from the middle ear to the nasopharynx¤Inner ear has three areasnSemicircular canals -associated with equilibriumnVestibule-associated with equilibriumnCochlea–associated with hearing
explanation: The human ear is divided into three structural regions: 1) Outer ear: consisting of the pinna and the auditory canal. 2) Middle ear: begins at the tympanic membrane (eardrum) and ends at the oval and round windows. It houses the three small ossicles: malleus (hammer), incus (anvil), and stapes (stirrup). The auditory (Eustachian) tube connects the middle ear to the nasopharynx to equalize pressure. 3) Inner ear: contains the fluid-filled semicircular canals (rotational equilibrium), vestibule (gravitational equilibrium), and the cochlea (hearing).

questions.q: What are the three middle ear bones (ossicles), listed in order of sound transmission?
questions.exp: Vibrations travel from the tympanic membrane to the malleus, then the incus, and finally the stapes.

questions.q: Which structure of the inner ear is specialized for hearing?
questions.exp: The cochlea is the snail-shaped structure of the inner ear that contains receptors for hearing, while the vestibule and semicircular canals handle equilibrium.

original_text: Senses of Hearing and Balance¨The Auditory Canal and Middle Ear¤Sound waves enter the auditory canal¤Sound waves strike the tympanic membrane, causing it to vibratenMalleus takes pressure from inner surface of tympanic membranenPasses it via the incus to the stapes, multiplying the pressure along the waynStapes strikes the membrane of oval window, passing pressure to fluid within the cochlea¨Inner Ear¤Spiral organ (organ of Corti) contains hair cells that synapse with nerve fibers of the cochlear nerve¤Mechanoreceptors for sound are the hair cells of the cochlear canalnSound causes the basilar membrane to vibratenThe stereocilia of the hair cells bendnNerve impulses begin in the cochlear nerve and travel to the brain stem, then to the auditory center of the cerebral cortex
explanation: Sound waves enter the auditory canal and vibrate the tympanic membrane. The malleus, incus, and stapes transmit and amplify this pressure, with the stapes striking the oval window. This creates pressure waves in the cochlear fluid, causing the basilar membrane of the spiral organ (organ of Corti) to vibrate. This vibration bends the stereocilia of sensory hair cells (the mechanoreceptors for sound). Bending of the stereocilia generates nerve impulses that travel along the cochlear nerve to the brain stem, and then to the auditory cortex.

questions.q: How is sound amplified within the middle ear?
opts: The auditory canal contracts to focus air.
The three ossicles (malleus, incus, stapes) multiply pressure as they transmit vibrations to the oval window.
The Eustachian tube active-transports sound waves.
The hair cells release norepinephrine into the middle ear.
questions.exp: The physical arrangement and leverage of the middle ear ossicles amplify sound pressure waves before they reach the inner ear.

questions.q: What is the sensory organ containing the mechanoreceptors (hair cells) for hearing?
opts: The spiral organ (organ of Corti) in the cochlea
questions.exp: The spiral organ (organ of Corti) within the cochlea houses the sensory hair cells that convert fluid vibrations into nerve impulses.

questions.q: What cellular event directly initiates nerve impulses in the cochlear nerve?
opts: The breakdown of glycogen in the middle ear
The bending of the hair cells' stereocilia as the basilar membrane vibrates
The fusion of rod cells with the choroid
The flow of lymph into the shoulder region
questions.exp: Bending of the stereocilia on hair cells opens ion channels, depolarizing the cell and initiating nerve impulses along the cochlear nerve.

original_text: Senses of Hearing and Balance¨Mechanoreceptors for Equilibrium¨Rotational Equilibrium¤Ampullae of semi-circular canal contain hairs¤Shift when rotational force occursnSends nerve impulse to vestibular nerve¨Gravitational Equilibrium¤Utricle and saccule contain hair cells¤When head bends, hairs shift in the membrane fluidnSends nerve impulse to vestibular nerveThe different nerve impulses let the brain know head orientation at all times
explanation: The inner ear contains mechanoreceptors for two types of balance: 1) Rotational Equilibrium: detects angular or rotational acceleration. The ampullae (swollen bases) of the semicircular canals contain hair cells that bend when head rotation causes fluid movement, sending impulses via the vestibular nerve. 2) Gravitational Equilibrium: detects straight-line acceleration and head position relative to gravity. The utricle and saccule within the vestibule contain hair cells. When the head bends or accelerates, hair cells shift in the membrane fluid, sending impulses along the vestibular nerve.

questions.q: What structures sense rotational (angular) equilibrium?
opts: The cochlea and organ of Corti
The semicircular canals (specifically within the ampullae)
The tympanic membrane and Eustachian tube
The lateral line system and ommatidia
questions.exp: Rotational equilibrium is detected by hair cells located in the ampullae at the base of the semicircular canals.

questions.q: Which chambers of the vestibule detect gravitational equilibrium (straight-line movement and head tilt)?
questions.exp: The utricle and saccule are the two chambers of the vestibule that detect linear acceleration and gravity.

explanation: Somatic senses have receptors in the skin, muscles, joints, and internal organs (viscera): 1) Proprioceptors: mechanoreceptors in muscles and joints involved in reflex actions maintaining muscle tone (e.g., muscle spindles and Golgi tendon organs). 2) Cutaneous receptors: specialized structures in the skin that detect touch, pressure, pain, and temperature (e.g., Meissner corpuscles, Pacinian corpuscles, Merkel disks, Ruffini endings, and Krause end bulbs). 3) Pain receptors (nociceptors): free nerve endings that generate nerve impulses when stimulated by chemicals released by damaged cells, interpreted by the brain as pain.

questions.q: What are proprioceptors, and what is an example?
opts: Sensory cells for smell; olfactory bulb
Receptors in muscles and joints that maintain muscle tone; muscle spindles and Golgi tendon organs
Rods and cones in the fovea centralis
questions.exp: Proprioceptors are mechanoreceptors that monitor muscle length and tension (like muscle spindles and Golgi tendon organs) to regulate muscle tone.

questions.q: What type of receptor is a pain receptor, and how does it detect injury?
opts: Myelinated Pacinian corpuscles; detects mechanical stretch
Free nerve endings (nociceptors); stimulated by chemicals released from damaged cells
Ommatidia units; stimulated by UV light wavelengths
Bipolar cells; stimulated by calcium influx
questions.exp: Pain receptors are free nerve endings (nociceptors) that detect chemicals released from injured or damaged cells.
